"Is Social Security taxable?" is one of the most common tax questions retirees ask — and the answer frustrates almost everyone: it depends. Depending on your total income, anywhere from 0% to 85% of your Social Security benefits can be subject to federal income tax. The tax was introduced in 1983, originally affecting about 10% of recipients. Today, because the income thresholds were never indexed for inflation, roughly 56% of Social Security recipients pay tax on their benefits.

The good news: even in the worst case, you'll never pay tax on 100% of your Social Security. The bad news: the formula for calculating the taxable amount is one of the most convoluted in the entire tax code. In this guide, we'll break it down into plain English, show you exactly how to calculate what you owe, and — most importantly — share strategies the FI community uses to reduce or eliminate the tax entirely.

The IRS uses a special formula called "combined income" (also called "provisional income") to determine how much of your Social Security benefits are taxable. Here's the formula:

Combined Income = Adjusted Gross Income (AGI) + Nontaxable Interest + Half of Social Security Benefits

The resulting number determines which taxation tier you fall into. Notice that the thresholds haven't changed since 1993 — they are not adjusted for inflation, which means more retirees cross into taxable territory every year.

Important: "Up to 85% taxed" does not mean you pay an 85% tax rate. It means 85% of your benefits are added to your taxable income and taxed at your ordinary income rate. If you're in the 22% bracket and 85% of your $30,000 benefit is taxable, you'd owe 22% on $25,500 — roughly $5,610.

This is the most common Social Security tax confusion. When the IRS says "up to 85% of benefits are taxable," it means 85% of your benefit amount gets added to your taxable income and taxed at your regular rate. If your marginal rate is 22% and 85% of your $30,000 benefit is taxable, you owe about $5,610 — not $25,500. The effective tax rate on your full benefit in this example is about 18.7%.

Let's walk through a real example. Meet Sarah: she's 67, single, retired, and receives $24,000 per year in Social Security benefits. She also has $18,000 in IRA withdrawals and $2,000 in municipal bond interest.

Step 2: Determine the Tier Sarah is single with combined income of $32,000, which falls between $25,000 and $34,000. She's in the 50% tier — up to 50% of her benefits may be taxable.

Step 3: Calculate the Taxable Amount The actual calculation involves comparing two formulas and taking the lesser amount. For the 50% tier:

Sarah adds $3,500 to her other taxable income. At a 12% marginal rate, that's roughly $420 in additional federal tax on her Social Security.

Beyond federal taxes, 13 states also tax Social Security benefits to some degree as of 2026. Each state has its own thresholds and exemption amounts:

The remaining 37 states and Washington, D.C. do not tax Social Security benefits at all. If you're planning where to retire, this is a meaningful factor — especially if you have substantial SS benefits combined with other retirement income.

The FI community has identified several strategies that can significantly reduce the tax bite on Social Security benefits. The key insight: since taxation is based on combined income, controlling your income in retirement is the lever.

This is the single most powerful strategy. Roth IRA withdrawals are not included in the combined income formula. If you retire early (before Social Security age), you have a window of low-income years to convert Traditional IRA/401(k) money to Roth.

Example: Between ages 55 and 67, you convert $500,000 from your Traditional IRA to a Roth — paying tax at rates as low as 10-12%. When you claim Social Security at 67, your Roth withdrawals don't push you into a higher SS taxation tier. Instead of 85% of your benefits being taxable, you might pay tax on 0-50%.

The math is dramatic over a 25+ year retirement. Converting at 12% during early retirement to avoid 22%+ taxation on Social Security for decades produces enormous tax savings.

Every dollar of AGI pushes you toward the 50% or 85% taxation tiers. Strategic levers include:

Once you reach age 70.5, you can donate up to $105,000 per year directly from your IRA to a qualified charity. This satisfies your Required Minimum Distribution (RMD) without the distribution being included in your AGI. Lower AGI means lower combined income, which means less Social Security is taxable.

For charitably inclined retirees, QCDs are one of the most tax-efficient giving strategies available — they simultaneously reduce your income tax AND reduce the tax on your Social Security benefits.

Delaying Social Security from 62 to 70 increases your benefit by roughly 77%. But there's a secondary benefit: during the delay years, you have more room to do Roth conversions at low tax rates without Social Security benefits adding to your combined income. The combination of larger benefits and lower taxation on those benefits makes delay doubly powerful for tax optimization.

If you retire before claiming Social Security, you have a golden window for Roth conversions. With little or no earned income and no SS benefits, you can convert Traditional IRA money to Roth at the lowest tax brackets of your lifetime. Every dollar you convert is a dollar that will never increase the tax on your Social Security benefits. This window closes permanently once you start claiming.

A step-by-step walkthrough for estimating what you owe.

List your AGI from all sources: IRA/401(k) withdrawals, pension income, wages, dividends, capital gains, rental income. Get your total Social Security benefit from your SSA-1099 form.

Pro tip: Don't forget nontaxable municipal bond interest — it counts in the combined income formula even though it's not on your 1040.

Add your AGI + nontaxable interest + half of your Social Security benefits. This "combined income" number determines your taxation tier.

Compare your combined income to the thresholds: Single — $25K (50% tier), $34K (85% tier). Married filing jointly — $32K (50% tier), $44K (85% tier).

For the 50% tier: take 50% of combined income above the lower threshold (capped at 50% of benefits). For the 85% tier: the calculation is more complex — use IRS Publication 915 worksheet or tax software.

Pro tip: Tax software handles this automatically. If doing it by hand, IRS Publication 915 has the complete worksheet.

The taxable portion of your Social Security gets added to your other taxable income and taxed at your marginal rate. Check if your state also taxes Social Security.

For single filers, Social Security becomes partially taxable when combined income exceeds $25,000 (50% tier) and up to 85% taxable above $34,000. For married filing jointly, the thresholds are $32,000 (50% tier) and $44,000 (85% tier). These thresholds have not changed since 1993 and are not indexed for inflation.

No. Social Security benefits are not earned income. They are classified as unearned income for tax purposes. This distinction matters for things like the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC), IRA contribution eligibility, and the Social Security earnings test (which only applies to earned income like wages and self-employment).

No — and this is why Roth accounts are so powerful in retirement. Roth IRA withdrawals are not included in the combined income formula used to determine Social Security taxation. Converting Traditional IRA money to Roth before claiming Social Security can dramatically reduce the tax on your benefits for life.

Yes. File Form W-4V with the Social Security Administration to have federal income tax withheld from your benefits. You can choose 7%, 10%, 12%, or 22% withholding. This avoids the surprise of a large tax bill at filing time. State tax withholding varies by state.

Social Security benefits are included in the Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI) calculation that determines Medicare Part B and Part D premium surcharges (IRMAA). High-income retirees can pay significantly more for Medicare — up to 3.4 times the standard premium. Managing MAGI in retirement affects both Social Security taxation and Medicare costs.

There have been numerous proposals to reform Social Security taxation, including indexing the thresholds for inflation, raising the taxable percentage above 85%, or eliminating the tax entirely. As of 2026, no changes have been enacted. The thresholds have remained unchanged since 1993, meaning inflation automatically pushes more retirees into taxable territory each year.

Yes, Social Security benefits can be taxable — up to 85% of your benefits may be added to your taxable income depending on your combined income. The thresholds are low ($25,000 single, $32,000 married) and haven't been adjusted for inflation since 1993, catching more retirees every year. The single most powerful strategy is Roth conversions during early retirement years before claiming Social Security. Every dollar in a Roth account is a dollar that won't push your Social Security into the taxable zone. Plan your retirement income sources deliberately, and you can reduce or eliminate this tax entirely.

#8990. The Best Tri Suits for Postpartum Bodies (That Actually Offer Support)

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Gearing up for your first triathlon postpartum, you’ve certainly got a lot on your mind. Most of it probably has nothing to do with you. Who will take care of your child for so many hours? What will they eat? Are they going to miss nap time? Still, you’ll need to make sure that you have all the right equipment and fuel laid out the night before the race.

And while there might not be a “postpartum” filter on triathlon brands’ websites, it’s worth looking into purchasing a new tri suit to accommodate and support the same evolving body that has nourished both you and baby over the past few years.

If you’re still lactating and plan on expressing milk during the race, finding a tri kit with good access is especially crucial. Many mothers have publicly pumped milk while racing (if you’re thinking of doing the same, read my tips for why (and how) new moms should breastfeed during a triathlon).

One common refrain among lactating athletes is that we need more appropriate gear to better facilitate mid-race expression. In testing these tri suits, I therefore paid special attention to how easy each one was to unzip and slip a breast pump inside. That usually hinged on how deep a suit’s zipper was and if it had sleeves. Of course, it also helps to have a nursing sports bra underneath. And because you may be required to carry a hand pump the entire length of a race, I also noted whether pockets were spacious enough to accommodate such equipment.

Not every mother expresses milk, however. That’s why I examined several other aspects of these suits that specifically impact postpartum bodies. For starters, compression. At 2 ½ years postpartum, my body still doesn’t look like it did before baby, and compression in a tri suit can aid in keeping everything from feeling “loose.” However, if you find tight suits restrictive to your airways or range of motion, you might look for the suits with fewer stars in that category.

I also focused on how easy it is to pull each suit down for bathroom breaks (sorry, coach, but there’s gonna be more of them in motherhood). And while chafing is always a concern among triathletes, you might find yourself chafing more and/or in different places as your body fat redistributes itself postpartum. Of course, in addition to all these factors, I rated suits according to more traditional criteria like durability and fit.

Again, don’t simply go for the suit with the most stars. Consider your unique needs, and try suits on before ripping off the tags in excitement. This article is meant to offer helpful insights as you return to racing postpartum, but as you know by now, every mom’s journey is different. What matters most is that you return to the start line on your own time and in your own style.

Size options: XXS, XS, S, M, L, XL Styles: Sleeveless, Sleeved, Tank, Shorts

If you’re just getting back into racing postpartum, a sprint triathlon may be first on your agenda. There are suits designed for that, including the 2XU Core Tri Suit. I wouldn’t wear this for a half or full Ironman — there aren’t enough pockets to store nutrition, and while the padding is high-quality, it’s also minimal. But it’s an excellent option for shorter races, as long as you’re fine with a looser fit. Plus, this suit is relatively easy on the wallet, which can come as a blessing since child-rearing is financially difficult enough.

Former competitive swimmers will understand me when I say this suit is more like an Aquablade than a Fastskin in terms of compression. Some postpartum women will appreciate the looser belly fit, as well as the fact that this suit will accommodate some amount of weight fluctuation and body recomposition as you get back into racing. Even so, the extra folds of fabric did nothing to help the already subpar breathability of this suit. The midriff trapped heat and sweat more than any other suit I’ve ever worn. I was asked to determine if any of these suits were “swamp-assy,” and this one certainly leaned that way. Still, I loved how the open back made me feel like I wasn’t wearing anything at all on my shoulders.

For those concerned about lactation, the zipper of this suit didn’t zip down far enough to accommodate easy breastfeeding or pumping. For shorter distances, though, that’s likely not an issue. The top of the zipper reached unusually high, touching the base of my neck, and it chafed me slightly on the run. Finally, a few loose threads along the seams concerned me about how this suit would hold up across more than one racing season.

Size options: XS, S, M, L, XL, 2XL Styles: Sleeved, Sleeveless, Jersey, Shorts

I wanted to like this suit so that I could rock its floral design at my next Ironman, but I had to knock off several stars because of the terrible chafing it caused in my armpits. That’s not a problem I usually experience, even with sleeved tri suits, but I couldn’t even finish a 3-mile run without my skin screaming in pain. I even felt the suit chafing me while swimming.

It seems I’m not alone, either; I recently spoke to someone else who has suffered unusual chafing in the armpits from a Zoot suit. Nevertheless, there are plenty of folks who peel off this suit after a race and find themselves untarnished, so it’s worth trying on for size (or simply opting for the sleeveless version). Keep in mind that if you’re recently postpartum and had a C-section, the high waistline might irritate the scar.

What I most loved about this suit (aside from its aesthetics) was its full frontal zipper, making dressing and undressing a breeze. My breasts aren’t small, and yet, I had no difficulty cajoling the zipper up or down. Furthermore, you could easily let the top portion of this suit hang loose while breastfeeding a baby. I also appreciated the numerous pockets, though they weren’t very spacious. The cooling pockets, found on the neck and kidney area, were the cherry on top of what was already great breathability.

Size options: XS, S, M, L, XL, 2XL, 3XL Styles: Sleeved, Sleeveless, Sleeved top, Tank top, Shorts

This suit struck the perfect balance between price and performance, and it especially stood out for its medium-high, yet comfortable, level of compression. Because it’s sleeveless and features a full frontal zipper, it’s relatively easy to pull on and take off – whether that’s to pump milk or to hit the restroom. Still, the upper-body compression meant that the zipper was a little harder to tug up over a larger breast size. Plus, the top of the zipper chafed me slightly while running – the protective flap should have been larger.

If you’ve ever complained about how minuscule girl pockets are, this suit will please you with its two large hip pockets, each of which could fit an item as large as a handheld breast pump (or extra chamois butter if you find yourself chafing more postpartum). Those are in addition to two smaller, though still relatively sizable, pockets on the back.

For the most part, this is a great option if you feel like elite suits restrict your airways or range of motion. It performed spectacularly in the water due to its flexibility and sleeveless nature. I also loved how securely the grippers glued the shorts portion to my legs so that they never rode up. Even so, this suit felt slightly tight across my back as I cycled, especially because I hunch slightly more than is good for me.

Size options: XS, S, ST, M, MT, L, LT, XL Available styles: Short sleeve, Sleeveless, Short sleeve tri top, Sleeveless tri top, Tri shorts

This suit fit so snugly and comfortably that I had difficulty finding anything to criticize. I typically don’t love sleeved suits, but the thin, breathable fabric on this one made me forget that I was going rogue. It’s high on the compression factor, which is ideal if you want more core support and to shave off every second possible from your time. Still, the sleeves were flexible and loose enough to allow full range of motion.

Did I wish that this suit came in something other than black or black-and-white? Yes. Not only because a bit of brightness cheers me up when I feel like puking on the run course, but also because my personal cheerleading squad can spot me from a greater distance when I’m wearing bright colors. Still, they say black is classy, so I’m willing to hang up my dreams of a tie-dye race suit for a little while longer. That said, I did notice a bit of color leaking out of the suit once while handwashing it.

The full frontal zipper will be easy to negotiate for those with smaller breasts, but if yours are naturally larger or engorged from breastfeeding, be prepared to possibly spend a few extra seconds aligning and jostling it up. Finally, you won’t be able to overpack with this suit; the two back pockets are medium at best and diagonally aligned.

#8986. It’s Nia Long’s Moment—Again

There is a specific kind of vertigo that comes with leaving a movie theater in the middle of the day. The world is suddenly too bright, too loud, and slightly unreal. You have, after all, been inside someone else’s carefully constructed reality for two hours. And then you’re back outside, blinking into the afternoon light, not quite returned to yourself, the movie still clinging to you like perfume. It’s in this particular state that I meet Nia Long for an early lunch in a quiet corner at the Chateau Marmont.

I have just seen Michael (the new Michael Jackson biopic) a month ahead of its April release. I’m still thinking about the film when Long, who plays Jackson family matriarch Katherine Jackson, arrives looking chic but low-key in an oversized blazer, wide-leg jeans, and a Miu Miu baseball cap pulled low. As we ease ourselves into the conversation, I’m struck by the strange doubling effect of the movie vertigo: the woman before me and the woman I have just watched, layered like two transparencies held up to the light.

On screen, Long plays Katherine Jackson with a studied stillness. The first time we see her, watching her boys rehearse, the frame holds on her loving face for just a few beats. She says almost nothing. She doesn’t have to. Juxtaposed to Colman Domingo’s blustering portrayal of Joe Jackson and Jaafar Jackson’s uncanny performance as his late uncle Michael, Long has found a way to make silence load-bearing. Restraint is the most visible thing in any scene she occupies.

In person she seems the opposite of restrained. She is blunt but also quite warm, with a dry sense of humor and a deep well of emotional intelligence. She is very much a Scorpio. She notices everything. And, in playing Mrs. Jackson (who is still with us at the age of 95), Long has tapped into the part of herself that knows how to let silence do the work. The word she reaches for when she talks about the experience of playing the matriarch—a word she will return to several times during our conversation—is grace.

“There have been moments in my life where I’ve been required to be more graceful than I’ve ever had to be in the past,” she says. “And that requires a sense of really being able to dig deep into some sort of self-examination. Like, what do I stand for? What’s important to me, ultimately, regardless of Hollywood, the noise? And number one, for me personally, my children come before anything. And so I think when you look at Michael’s journey, and you look at Katherine’s journey, the only way you thrive and survive is through a tremendous amount of grace.” She pauses. “What I think I learned from her is that sometimes grace is really quiet.”

Long occupies a place in our cultural memory that few actors do. She is, for a certain generation, the platonic ideal of ’90s Fine, a phrase that’s not only about beauty or aesthetic but also about a certain feeling. Watching her as Nina in Love Jones or Jordan in The Best Man or Lisa in The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air, you conjure up a place and time and attitude that feels synonymous with Long. Of course, there is the image, and then there is the human sitting across from me, eating her go-to order of salmon with a side of mustard. And as she does, I ask what she thinks about the iconography and the nostalgia that surrounds her.

“My commitment to work is not for accolades or attention, or even to be famous, quite honestly,” she says. “But I do think because of my commitment to truth and purpose, there is a thing, and I don’t know what that thing is, that people see in my work. And it makes them feel good. It makes them feel inspired. It makes them feel like they know me.”

In a fickle Hollywood landscape that’s even more fickle when it comes to Black actors, Long doesn’t take the longevity and love she’s cultivated for granted. “There's highs and lows,” Long admits. “I’m having a great year, but I don’t know what’s happening next year.”

Long has starred in several iconic Black films, and she’s always been intentional about how she plays her characters. Much like with the Katherine Jackson role, she creates a version of the person that feels, to her, like something true.

“The only strategy I have in this game is my bank account. Let’s strategize how we’re going to make money and create generational wealth. That is where I’m strategic.” She laughs, scratches her palm. “My hand just started itching the minute I said money. That’s a good thing. Maybe something’s happening. Something’s coming.”

Once she’s in it, though, the work becomes something more personal. “I work hard to make sure that when I represent us, it’s not just someone putting their agenda on me. Whether it’s my hair, my makeup, my wardrobe, my lines.”

Now that her eldest son is in his 20s and her youngest son, 14, is old enough to stay home by himself, the actor feels ready to expand in all directions. She wants to continue to produce more films, craft new stories both behind and in front of the camera. She tells me about a new film she’s just wrapped shooting in New York, Don’t Ever Wonder, a romantic dramedy (“If that even exists anymore”) three years in the making. It will feature her onscreen reunion with Love Jones leading man Larenz Tate. Directed by Eugene Ashe and featuring an ensemble that includes Blair Underwood, Susan Kelechi Watson, and Algee Smith, the film is all about second acts.

“This is not a continuation of Love Jones,” she emphasizes. “This is a continuation of love, and of what happens once you’ve had your kids, they’re off to college, and you’re empty nesters. And that’s kind of where the story begins. There’s a lot of funny and there’s a lot of heartbreak, and I think it’s a really honest story.”

In talking to Long, I get the sense that honesty and truth is what she values most in the stories she tells. It’s what she values in life as well. Perhaps that’s what compels me, somewhere in the middle of our lunch, to unmask. I mention that I am conducting the interview a little out of sorts, having just ended a 12-year relationship.

“Okay, but when was it really over?” she asks.

"You didn’t have to gag me like that!" I say.

She laughs. I tell her that I am trying to imagine what life will look like—what I will look like—on the other side of this break-up. That’s when the idea of grace comes up again.

In 2022, Long went through that peculiar part of fame where something private becomes public overnight: her partner’s cheating scandal that resulted in the end of their 13-year relationship. She doesn’t have to go too deep into it if she doesn’t want to, I assure her, but the actor doesn’t shy away. On the other side of the experience with her ex, with whom she now has a healthy coparenting relationship, she has an unflinching clarity about the whole ordeal.

“The amount of pouring into myself that I’ve done is strong and mighty and intentional. I’ve now identified the things that I need to work on and the things that I need to heal. But I have also identified what is intolerable.”

That clarity has been hard-won. When the cheating scandal happened, there was a groundswell of support from fans, a protectiveness over Long as a woman and as a cultural touchstone. But in the instances that she’s talked publicly about it, including in our conversation, I’m struck by how her gratitude for the support is always tempered with nuance.

“I’m proud of myself for giving so much grace. For being able to say people make mistakes and things happen. It’s life. When the stakes are high, the news is big. I can’t do anything about that, but I don’t have to protect my ego in any of this.” She says all this very matter-of-factly, which is the only way she seems capable of saying things.

In the same straightforward tone she suggests I write out everything I need to say to my ex without sending it, because ultimately “it’s not about another person’s behavior. It’s about your bottom line and the magnitude in which you’re committed to self-love,” she says. “I don’t think it's healthy to hold onto things because then you’re just walking around with this burdensome energy. It could be writing it down. It could be meditation. It could be prayer. There’s a lot of ways to manage the noise. But you don’t have to respond to the noise with the undercurrent of your own trauma.”

I write down this last sentence because it is useful, but also because it is the key to something I’ve been watching Long do across the whole of our conversation: find the lesson in whatever she is given.

Long is working on her first memoir, a process she describes as one of the “biggest, bravest, challenging” things she’s ever done. It’s been a two-year process, a constant negotiation with her own relationship to letting go.

“I can read something I wrote two years ago and go: ‘Oh no, that’s not actually how I feel about that now.’” Long’s father, Doughtry Long Jr., a poet who died in 2020, told her the hardest thing about writing is knowing when to stop. “And I’m like: When is that going to happen? Because I haven’t gotten there yet.”

The memoir takes her back to Iowa City, where she spent six years of her childhood while her mother attended university. She was born in Brooklyn, in a Trinidadian household where everyone on the block was Black. Living in the Midwest during her formative years, she encountered few other Black girls, which disoriented her relationship to race.

“In writing this memoir, I realized the impact that experience had on my own view of beauty,” she says. “And my own self-acceptance of being a pretty brown-skinned little girl growing up in Iowa. I thought I was beautiful because my mother said it and my family said it, but the world told me something different.” She lets that sit. “So to now be a face for Estée Lauder, it’s kind of ironic, because I didn’t feel beautiful until Black Hollywood said I was beautiful.”

That an entire generation of Black women found a reflection of Black beauty in Nia Long while Long herself was still waiting to see it tells us something about how beauty standards work, and how much labor goes into transforming them. Nineties Fine, after all, did not emerge from a vacuum. It was a corrective, Black Hollywood’s answer to a century of the larger industry rendering Black women invisible or, worse, making us visible in ways that were wholly out of our control. Long’s most iconic characters—and indeed, Long herself—reflected a new idea of beauty, of the Black leading lady, expansive in some ways and still restrictive in others. Now, some 30 years on, Long embodies a new facet of being a Black woman in Hollywood.

“Black don’t crack” gets lobbed at Black women constantly, ostensibly as a compliment, but one that sometimes erases the very real pressure that comes with aging—especially aging on a public stage, especially when people have a particular image of you stored in amber.

But Long is not interested in pretending that the body is not a thing that transforms. “I’m 55. I got hormonal stuff going. Your body shifts, changes. It’s a whole new body.” She is not wistful about this. She also ate the truffle parmesan fries and does not appear remotely conflicted about it. She mentions the coming press tour for Michael, how she wants to be in beautiful gowns but she also wants French fries.

“I don’t deprive myself of anything that I want,” she says. “I find the balance.”

Beauty was never her primary currency, she says. It had to be something else, other inheritances: her father’s curiosity, her mother’s fierce self-possession. Tattooed and free-spirited, her mother wore leg warmers in the middle of summer because they matched her outfit, and she did not care for one second what anyone thought about that. Embarrassed, Long would beg her mother to take them off. She never did. As an adult, Long sees the power and freedom in that.

Our plates are carted away. Long has to leave soon for a pizza party at home with her youngest son and his friends. Before she goes, I ask her what freedom, at this point, is to her.

“Being able to do what you want to do when you want to do it, because it serves your spirit, not what everyone else thinks you need to be or should be,” she says. That type of freedom, Long adds, doesn’t require an audience.“You don’t have to have anyone else’s permission to do what you love. And it doesn’t have to be on the big stage. It could be in your kitchen. I know I have freedom right now to make a pizza. I’m going to do it.”

Photographer: Emmanuel Sanchez MonsalveStylist: Dione DavisSet Design: Henrique CirilonetoHair: Naeemah LafondMakeup: Keita MooreManicurist: Sonya MeeshWriter: Zeba Blay

#8980. How to ‘Quiet Quit’ Your Mom

You’re probably familiar with the term quiet quitting. For a while, that little phrase has been used to describe the experience of executing the bare minimum at work without actually leaving your job: You do just enough to get by but never rise above that benchmark to prove yourself or exceed expectations. It’s a strategy that can keep you employed while preserving your mental and emotional energy.

The term has since been applied to other parts of life, like relationships. And, yes, it could also apply to the one you have with your mom. Though you’re probably not collecting paychecks here, maintaining a relationship with your mother may connect you to important resources you need to get by. Maybe your mom really does play a big role in your finances, or she’s your source of health insurance. She could also be a connection to your culture or other family members that you don’t want to distance yourself from. Logistics aside, you might just want some distance from your mom without sacrificing your emotional connection. As I learned from reporting my book Motherf*cked: How to Keep Your Mother’s Toxic Drama From Ruining Your Life, those are all solid reasons to maintain a relationship that leaves you exhausted.

Going low-contact is pretty much what it sounds like: staying in touch with minimal contact. However, there’s no official definition, therapist Whitney Goodman, LMFT, told me in an interview for Motherf*cked. For some, it could look like avoiding one-on-one visits but checking in via text, email, quarterly phone calls, or greeting cards. Or you could catch up in person while avoiding the details of your life. The frequency of low-contact contact varies too. Some would say talking once a week is low-contact for them. Others might say once a year.

The reasons why people go low-contact differ as much as the ways it can look. Generally speaking, taking space can be useful anytime a relationship feels painful or draining. It gives you more time, energy, and emotional bandwidth to take care of yourself and tend to other important parts of your life.

That can be especially helpful in our relationships with our moms, a dynamic that, for many reasons, is often packed with emotional triggers. If spending time with your mom feels exhausting, you’re sick of always stressing about this relationship, or you’ve tried and failed to set boundaries with her in the past, pulling back might be helpful here, Goodman says. If you can relate, here’s how to do that.

Ideally, this process is a series of experiments where you pull back from the relationship in different ways to see what feels good and what doesn’t, Goodman explains. You can then use that information to determine how much contact is too much—or not enough. Here’s how to get started.

Going low-contact is really just setting a boundary, or defining what behavior you will or won’t tolerate. You’re showing others how you want to be treated. Sometimes, people don’t like being restricted and get messy when limits are put on their relationships. Moms can be like that too.

If you’ve already tried to set boundaries with your mom by, say, not answering every one of her calls or telling her that you don’t want to talk about your dating life, now is a good time to reflect on how that went.

Moms who are receptive to those guardrails may be easygoing about any additional boundaries. That could mean you don’t need to cut as many points of contact to feel better about the relationship. On the other hand, if your mom has blown through your boundaries in the past, you might need stronger limitations to protect your peace today. Keep that in mind for the next step.

Again, there is no official criterion defining a low-contact relationship, so don’t get hung up on labels. First, think about how much contact you have now. How often do you spend time together? What does that time look like? What would you change to make this relationship less taxing?

Maybe you see your mom every Sunday, let her come over unannounced, and answer all of her texts—even the ones you’d rather not. Consider which of these interactions take the most out of you, and ask yourself, Would eliminating this point of contact make the relationship less exhausting overall?

You could start small by taking a beat to check in with yourself before responding to your mom’s texts. If you don’t feel like dealing with her at that moment, don’t. If that’s not enough to preserve your energy, maybe you can limit the number of texts you’ll respond to each day or week. You can always change it up later by removing another point of contact, like those unannounced visits, if you need more space (see step five).

You don’t have to formally announce that you’re going low-contact, but giving your mom a heads-up might be useful.

If you’re not worried about your safety and your quiet quitting tactics mean your mom has to change her behavior, then laying out your plans could make sense. Plus, explaining why you put them in place might help you resolve whatever is behind your decision to quiet quit this relationship.

That said, if your version of low-contact doesn’t require anything from your mom, you don’t need to tell her it’s happening, says Goodman. For example, you can hold back information about your life or avoid certain events without discussing it first.

Feel weird about this? I get that, but here’s something to think about: You’ve probably told your mom about the ways she’s hurt you many, many times before, says Goodman. Even if you haven’t explicitly pointed to every single occasion she hurt your feelings, your body language and tone of voice likely have conveyed how her actions impacted you. You may be tired of retelling those painful events, which is why you’d like to avoid another confrontation with your mom. So consider this your permission not to.

Still, your mom might notice you pulling back and ask what’s going on. If she does, you can tell her why you’re not getting into your dating life or attending the family reunion. You don’t have to, though. You’re welcome to make excuses or just say, “Yep, you’re right, I’m not doing that anymore.” You don’t owe her an explanation.

Goodman says the best way to tell how going low-contact is working for you is to check in with your emotions as much as possible. You can write them down in your journal, use a mood- or emotions-tracking app, or bring them up to your therapist.

Yes, the feelings you’re tracking can be related to your mom and quiet quitting her, but don’t forget about all the others, says Goodman. It might not be obvious which feelings are related to your maternal figure and which aren’t. After breaking patterns that existed for a long time, you might get a sense that something is off. Maybe you feel purposeless or lost. Maybe it’s like you forgot something on your way to the airport, but you don’t know what it is.

All of that is normal, says Goodman. So is feeling like you really miss your mom, even if you know you did the right thing. Of course, everyone’s situation is different. Maybe you don’t truly miss her, but miss the idea of a person she’ll never be. When quiet quitting is working, those feelings should come up less frequently and/or become less intense. At the same time, you’ll likely feel some relief. You could notice more peace in your life and more space to focus on things other than your mom.

You can always tweak how much contact you have with your mom. Ideally, this involves a continuous assessment of what’s working and what’s not. If the low-contact plan you’ve established feels sustainable and makes you less obsessive or overwhelmed by the relationship—and your mom is able to abide by your rules—you might have found a solution. Success!

If this version of quiet quitting doesn’t keep your mom from violating your boundaries, emotionally manipulating you, or still leaves you drained, anxious, or depressed, you could level up, says Goodman. That means starting back at step one and quitting other parts of your relationship until you reach a point that feels sustainable.

Remember, the goal is for you to feel less stressed about your interactions with your mom. By finding a routine that works for you, you can protect the parts of your relationship that you love and lose the rest.

#8978. What I Learned from Finishing a Triathlon When Everything Goes Wrong

Before the start of her second attempt at the Cowichan Challenge, Anna Rea had high hopes of besting her time from the previous year. (Photo: Courtesy Anna Rea)

For this article, a novice age-group triathlete shared, in her own words, her experience racing the Olympic-distance Cowichan Challenge Triathlon. Despite multiple setbacks, she received encouragement from volunteers and fellow racers to keep going, and has tried to apply that same perseverance to other areas of her life.

It was a perfect early summer morning. The forecast wasn’t too hot, the water was warm, and there was no hint of wind. I had fueled and hydrated the day before. I was well rested and ready. I had done the exact same race one year earlier, which was my first ever triathlon.

This time, I assumed I would be faster. I had to be. Any other outcome would feel like failure.

But within a few minutes of the race start, the rest of the swimmers were barely visible. I had recently done two private lessons with a swimming coach, during which I learned that my technique was broken. There was no time to properly address it before the race.

The swim took 53 minutes, so I was eager to make up some time on the ride. But after five minutes on my bike, just as I was finding my rhythm, my derailleur seized up, and I couldn’t move the pedals. This was defeat.

I tearfully walked my bike back toward transition. I assumed there was no helping this situation. I hadn’t taken my bike for a tune-up before the race. I had failed.

After 25 minutes of walking, a race volunteer spotted me and ran over. He tinkered with my bike for a couple minutes, and I secretly hoped he would confirm my fears – that the bike was broken and it was time to give up. An easy out.

But when he fixed my bike with a couple turns of an Allen key, my guts twisted with dread. He encouraged me to get back on the bike. I told him I had given up, but he told me I might as well keep going since there were still a couple hours until the cut-off time. I had already spent the money, trained, and showed up to the race — I had nothing to lose.

I was alone for most of the ride. I kept apologizing to the volunteers along the race course because I felt guilty that they had to wait for me. I didn’t think I would even start the run, but I kept my focus on the moment, on each corner and hill, until I was back at transition.

My sister, who had completed the sprint distance and was already finished, was waiting for me. I updated her on my situation and asked if she and my mom were OK with waiting until I finished. She said yes and encouraged me.

Then a race worker advised me that the race cut-off was in 52 minutes. He said there was no way I would make it in time and suggested I drop out. I told him I wanted to try, and I accepted that I would complete part of the run without support.

I started the run before I could change my mind. I had a hard time seeing the direction markers on the course. After a couple wrong turns, I was overwhelmed with the urge to give up. I cursed out loud, turned on my heel, and started walking back toward transition. But I immediately met the eyes of an athlete walking back to his vehicle, finisher medal hanging from his neck. He told me to keep going. I told him about my broken bike, the bad swim, not making the cut-off time, and running in the wrong direction. He encouraged me to go anyway, so I did.

I did most of the trail run alone. The race volunteers were supportive and stayed past the cut-off even though they didn’t have to. I was overwhelmed with gratitude, and this time saying thank you was easier than saying sorry.

I shouted curses on the run, stumbling over tree roots in my fatigue, fueled by frustration and determination. When I was 1 kilometer from the end, I almost passed out at a hydration station. I regrouped and kept moving.

Four hours and 15 minutes that felt like an eternity were suddenly coming to an end. I saw the finish line arch. I heard the applause as by now the awards ceremony was well underway. My sister saw me approaching, turned to a group of people behind her, and told them I was coming. And finally, after hours of exhaustion and frustration, wanting to give up the whole time, I crossed the finish line in front of a cheering crowd. And it was all worth it. I wouldn’t change a thing.

I’m not good at this. I don’t feel like I’m good at much. Genetic vision loss has greatly impacted the last few years of my life. I’m struggling to start a new career while managing chronic mental health issues and an acquired disability.

My confidence has taken a hit, and I think about giving up all the time. Things could be a lot worse – I have a support system and free healthcare in Canada. I am privileged with a great quality of life and generally good health aside from my eye disease.

But I feel behind. And by challenging myself to do things like triathlon, I expose myself to people who are incredibly fit. Self-criticism and body dysmorphia usually tag along.

The three months that have passed since that race have been difficult, and I feel out of touch with the person who persevered that day. I’m trying to let some light in and keep going – keep adapting to vision loss, keep building my career, and keep pushing myself.

I used to care a lot more about being good at things. Now I care about following through. Life is hard, and persisting when you don’t feel like enough is a feat of strength. I faced my fear of being slow that day and finished to a crowd of cheers. Of course I want to be faster. I want to finish in the pack. I want to be good at triathlon. But we can learn so much by being bad at things and doing them anyway.

Walking my bike back to the car, finisher medal around my neck, I turned to my sister and said, “Winning is cool, but losing is where it’s at.”

Do things you’re bad at. Challenge yourself. It’s OK if you don’t feel like a triathlete. How many things would you do if you weren’t afraid of failure?

#8977. Architecture and Neurodivergence: Designing for Different Ways of Perceiving Space

Wide doorways, properly designed ramps, and elevators are essential to a building's accessibility. But whether people can actually use its spaces also depends on the sensory conditions they offer. For some neurodivergent people, this is critical, as bright lights, overlapping sounds, or confusing circulation routes can prevent them from staying in a space and participating in activities.

#8975. Lacaton & Vassal Receives the 2027 Charlotte Perriand Award

Pritzker Prize laureates Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal have been announced as the recipients of the 2027 Le Prix Charlotte Perriand. Organized annually by the Créateurs Design Awards (CDA), the prize recognizes practitioners whose contributions have advanced architecture and design through a peer-led voting process. For its eighth edition, the organization highlighted the work of the French architectural studio as a demonstration of "how the adaptation of existing structures can improve living conditions while preserving resources and architectural heritage." Previous recipients of the prize include Xu Tiantian; Kazuyo Sejima and Ryue Nishizawa; Frida Escobedo; and Jeanne Gang.

Pritzker Prize laureates Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal have been announced as the recipients of the 2027 Le Prix Charlotte Perriand. Organized annually by the Créateurs Design Awards (CDA), the prize recognizes practitioners whose contributions have advanced architecture and design through a peer-led voting process. For its eighth edition, the organization highlighted the work of the French architectural studio as a demonstration of "how the adaptation of existing structures can improve living conditions while preserving resources and architectural heritage." Previous recipients of the prize include Xu Tiantian; Kazuyo Sejima and Ryue Nishizawa; Frida Escobedo; and Jeanne Gang.

Across 15 categories and two Legacy Awards, the Créateurs Design Awards program recognizes achievements in architecture, interior design, product design, curation, photography, journalism, digital art and related disciplines. This year, Lacaton & Vassal will be honored alongside Kengo Kuma, recipient of the Andrée Putman Lifetime Achievement Award 2027, with both distinctions bearing the names of influential French women whose work helped shape modern architecture and design. The Charlotte Perriand prize recognizes the duo's contribution to contemporary architecture "and their commitment to improving the quality of everyday life through the transformation and preservation of existing buildings."

Across 15 categories and two Legacy Awards, the Créateurs Design Awards program recognizes achievements in architecture, interior design, product design, curation, photography, journalism, digital art and related disciplines. This year, Lacaton & Vassal will be honored alongside Kengo Kuma, recipient of the Andrée Putman Lifetime Achievement Award 2027, with both distinctions bearing the names of influential French women whose work helped shape modern architecture and design. The Charlotte Perriand prize recognizes the duo's contribution to contemporary architecture "and their commitment to improving the quality of everyday life through the transformation and preservation of existing buildings."

The Award highlighted the care and imagination with which Lacaton & Vassal approach the places people call home, adding that their architecture shows how much can be gained by understanding what is already there. The practice was founded in 1989, after Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal finished their studies at the École Nationale Supérieure d'Architecture de Bordeaux. Notable works include the transformation of the Palais de Tokyo in Paris (2002 and 2012), the Nantes School of Architecture (2009), and the Cité du Grand Parc housing transformation in Bordeaux, completed with Frédéric Druot and Christophe Hutin, which shows how small, singular operations can have a significant infrastructural impact.

In the CDA's words, Lacaton & Vassal has "advanced an architectural approach grounded in spatial generosity, environmental responsibility and respect for the people who inhabit buildings" for more than three decades. The prize will be presented at a ceremony on January 16, 2027, at the Shangri-La Paris. Submissions for the 2027 Créateurs Design Awards remain open across 15 categories, with the deadline extended to November 22, 2026. The announcement adds to other recent recognitions worldwide, including Farshid Moussavi's 2026 Soane Medal for her contributions to architectural practice, history and theory, and Daniel Libeskind's 2026 Praemium Imperiale for Architecture. The second edition of the ArchDaily Student Project Awards is also now open for submissions, asking students around the world one question: What can architecture enable in the city?

#8974. Surrogacy Nearly Destroyed Our Marriage. It Also Brought Us Back

From the outside, our relationship looked the way it had for 24 years: solid.

After our first surrogacy experience ended in stillbirth, our friends were convinced we’d be fine because we were the “most together couple” they knew. I wasn’t so sure. For months, it had felt like my husband Ethan and I were two bodies fumbling to find each other in the dark. At home, our orbits rarely intersected. My eyes barely landed on Ethan. Once, he didn’t realize I was right behind him and he closed the door on me.

It felt like we were suspended in the quiet between the cracks and the crumble. We weathered life-altering challenges together in our 20s and 30s due to my whole-body symptoms from endometriosis, adenomyosis, early menopause, and a medical system that trivialized them all. My condition rattled our intimacy, upended my career, and made Ethan my caretaker. Being undiagnosed for decades also cost us my fertility, depleting my ovarian reserve and leading to miscarriage after miscarriage with IVF and IUIs.

Though we weren’t living the life we dreamed, and I felt guilty for the weight I foisted on Ethan, we managed to maintain the joie de vivre we’d had since we first met—until we turned to surrogacy.

Our decision to opt for an egg donor and a surrogate was an act of compromise. Though I’d always been ambivalent about motherhood, the idea of coparenting with Ethan had gradually filled me with tenderness and curiosity. But by then, after years of illness, I wanted a hysterectomy. Ethan still really wanted to be a dad. Neither of us wanted to jeopardize my wellness with more hormonal treatments and pregnancy losses, so we took what people called the “easy way out.” Though I was criticized by my doctors for giving up on my eggs and my uterus “too soon,” our decision to pursue surrogacy felt liberating—at first.

We thought finding a gestational surrogate would be the hardest part. Turns out, we were wrong. Instead, we were totally unprepared for the ways surrogacy was going to change our marriage.

Our first surrogacy experience was the kind we now caution other intended parents against. We entrusted an agency with our fate and our funds, putting them in charge of introducing us to a surrogate and acting as the intermediary who would reimburse her for pregnancy-related expenses on our behalf. At the time, we were unaware of their proven fraudulent history.

Not only were Ethan and I new to surrogacy, but we also felt vulnerable—maybe even desperate. We were privileged to have found someone who wanted to do this for us, and we wanted to be generous and grateful. You also don’t have much control when your baby is in someone else’s womb and your funds are in a corporation’s bank account. So we ignored the red flags we noticed with the agency’s inflated reimbursements and our surrogate’s jarring mood fluctuations.

If we’d shared our worries with each other early on, we may have had a chance to course-correct. At least I wouldn’t have felt so alone carrying this angst in my bones. At one of our second-trimester ultrasounds, I resented Ethan for being his jovial self while he talked to our active baby boy through the screen as I stood hunched against the wall, struggling to feel present. It wasn’t just that the pregnancy felt unbearably abstract for me as a mother who didn’t contribute her genes or her womb; I was also increasingly skeptical of the agency and walking on eggshells with our surrogate, who’d keep us at arm’s length one week and accuse us of not being supportive enough the next. I’d never gotten this far in a pregnancy and it should have been a happy time. Instead, I bottled up my distress and couldn’t breathe from the weight of it.

During our first surrogacy experience, Ethan let me bear the brunt of the conversations with our surrogate. He thought he had a supportive role, but his not being in the foreground put extra weight on my shoulders and took my time, energy, and headspace while sparing him. I was also the one who handled all the legal and financial paperwork, and the communication with the agency. Ethan was grateful and proud of me for managing what he considered more in my wheelhouse than his, but I felt paralyzing stress and resentment having to tackle these hard tasks on my own at such a vulnerable time.

Our breaking point was brought on by our different ways of grieving. While I naturally tend to dig deep into painful topics and emotions to make sense of them, Ethan prefers to compartmentalize. At the hospital after the delivery, Ethan preferred to leave the room when I stayed to spend a few minutes with our stillborn. I wanted the loss to feel more tangible, while he wanted to hold onto the joy from other memories, like when we saw him on ultrasounds. Neither of us was wrong, but we were disconnected.

The months that followed were agony because none of the doctors would counsel us on why our baby had died simply because I wasn’t the pregnant patient, as though we weren’t his parents and didn’t have the right to know. I spiraled into depression and was furious every time Ethan would tell his parents that we were fine. He didn’t want to burden them, but I didn’t want to mask our reality for the sake of others’ comfort. For 24 years—through long distance, sickness, and grief—we’d been the “strong couple” who never argued. Now, in the complexity of surrogacy, we kept snapping at each other because Ethan needed a semblance of normalcy and I needed to dwell in darkness.

So how do you come back to each other when who you were didn’t survive? Over nearly a year, thanks to our self-awareness, deep respect for one another, and therapy (which Ethan hated attending but did when required), we made three tiny shifts that saved our marriage.

When we met our second surrogate through a more ethical, transparent, and supportive agency that did not demand funds in trust, Ethan and I formed a true trio with her. It helped that she considered us a team and wanted our involvement in appointments, decisions, and her daily life. She’d use the word “together” so often that it initially triggered us; it felt so foreign to us after our first surrogacy journey, and we couldn’t tell which of the two experiences was the anomaly. Ethan made it a priority to participate in our conversations and replied to our group texts if I couldn’t. We all shared freely—our fears, dreams, victories, recipes, and silly inside jokes—and the three of us built an intimacy I never expected. When it was just the two of us, our surrogate was never far from our thoughts, as if our marriage had expanded to include her.

Ethan also started to help me with the challenging legal and financial tasks. He kept up with emails he was CC’ed on during the day and sat with me if we had paperwork to tackle, his hand on my back if I got overwhelmed.

When we lost our baby with our second surrogate at the end of the first trimester, we grieved as a unit. Our trio sat intertwined, our hands piled on my lap. At home, Ethan was more receptive to my needs on my bad days. Just watching him witness me in those moments, even if all he did was listen and sigh, brought us closer together. I was more understanding when he clung to his social activities to blow off steam. Ethan was more honest with family and friends about our emotional and financial distress. He agreed to ask for help and for a loan to help us get back on our feet after two surrogacy journeys and thirteen years of fertility and ongoing health expenses.

We decided not to talk about surrogacy on weekends or right before bed to give our nervous systems a chance to unwind. Dark humor helped us grieve: We’d sometimes whisper jaded comments to each other when triggered. When we imagine something creative we would have done with our kid, we say, “File it under never!” During the holidays, Ethan toasted me with, “Cheers to not losing a child this Christmas!” Holding space for our contrasting ways of grieving and meeting in the middle helped dissolve the resentment and tension between us.

Fertility treatments and surrogacy can become all-consuming for a couple, especially after decades of illness and loss. Being diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) after our first surrogacy experience further shook my identity. We started making a conscious effort to remember what was special about our life and our love before all this. We are more than what we carry and what we’ve lost.

Besides carving out periods of play, nature, and grief-free talk, we also pushed ourselves to keep money aside for leisure and travel—not just for our living expenses and surrogacy costs—so we can look forward to something in our calendar and savor new experiences together.

We found, though, that the least daunting way of rebuilding our future is to simply take care of our present. Often, all we can handle is the next half-hour: where to take a walk, what to make for supper, how to support each other right then. I worked hard to keep my eyes focused on Ethan until it became natural again. Even now, as we grapple with whether and how to continue with our surrogacy journey, when we start acting like passing ships because of our full heads and aching hearts, we drop everything, hug, touch.

I never expected our strong marriage to be impacted by the most tender gift we gave each other: the chance to grow our family through surrogacy. We’d naively thought what awaited us would be easier than the road that led there. Our experiences with surrogacy have changed how we show up for each other, both in joy and in grief.

I can’t say for certain that our marriage is now strong enough to survive anything that lies ahead. What I know is this: We’ve built what we’ll need to recalibrate our direction to find each other in the dark.

#8971. Designing Furniture to Outlast the Fit-Out

Furniture waste is not always the result of physical damage that renders a product unusable. Chairs, sofas, and tables are often discarded because they no longer fit an interior concept, are perceived as outdated, or are replaced during a renovation. In many cases, their structures remain functional, even when upholstery is worn, or the surrounding space has changed. The result is a cycle of replacement in which usable products become waste, while new resources are extracted and processed to manufacture their successors.

Furniture waste is not always the result of physical damage that renders a product unusable. Chairs, sofas, and tables are often discarded because they no longer fit an interior concept, are perceived as outdated, or are replaced during a renovation. In many cases, their structures remain functional, even when upholstery is worn, or the surrounding space has changed. The result is a cycle of replacement in which usable products become waste, while new resources are extracted and processed to manufacture their successors.

The environmental impact begins long before furniture reaches a landfill. Wood, metals, plastics, foams, and textiles require raw materials, processing, and energy to become finished products. A life cycle assessment of 25 furniture pieces across eight categories found that the pre-production stage, including raw material acquisition and processing, accounted for an average of 76% of the assessed environmental impact. The proportion varied between products, but the findings highlight the resources already invested in furniture by the time it reaches a building. When a product is discarded prematurely, the resources invested in its manufacture may not be fully utilized, while replacement creates demand for additional products and materials.

A life cycle assessment of 25 furniture pieces across eight categories found that the pre-production stage, including raw material acquisition and processing, accounted for an average of 76% of the assessed environmental impact. The proportion varied between products, but the findings highlight the resources already invested in furniture by the time it reaches a building. When a product is discarded prematurely, the resources invested in its manufacture may not be fully utilized, while replacement creates demand for additional products and materials.

For manufacturers, addressing this problem means considering what happens after furniture leaves their facilities. Approaches such as The Loop, a circular program by British furniture manufacturer Boss Design, connect product design with repair, reupholstery, reuse, redistribution, and material recovery. The aim is to create practical ways for furniture to stay in service as interiors and organizational needs change, while retaining the value of components that are still fit for use.

Approaches such as The Loop, a circular program by British furniture manufacturer Boss Design, connect product design with repair, reupholstery, reuse, redistribution, and material recovery. The aim is to create practical ways for furniture to stay in service as interiors and organizational needs change, while retaining the value of components that are still fit for use.

Furniture waste is partly a consequence of how products are purchased and managed. In commercial interiors, refurbishment can involve replacing entire furniture collections to achieve a new visual identity, even when individual pieces remain functional. Changes in workplace layouts, occupancy, and a space's intended use can also make existing furniture seem unsuitable. Without a practical way to adapt or redistribute it, replacement may become easier than renewal.

In commercial interiors, refurbishment can involve replacing entire furniture collections to achieve a new visual identity, even when individual pieces remain functional. Changes in workplace layouts, occupancy, and a space's intended use can also make existing furniture seem unsuitable. Without a practical way to adapt or redistribute it, replacement may become easier than renewal.

Design decisions influence whether alternatives are possible. Upholstered pieces, for example, combine components with different service lives. A frame may remain structurally sound after its fabric becomes worn, stained, or no longer matches a revised interior palette. If the upholstery cannot be removed and replaced independently, a relatively minor problem can lead to disposing of the entire piece. Replaceable upholstery, accessible fixings, and separable components make maintenance easier and may let furniture adapt to changes in appearance or use.

If the upholstery cannot be removed and replaced independently, a relatively minor problem can lead to disposing of the entire piece. Replaceable upholstery, accessible fixings, and separable components make maintenance easier and may let furniture adapt to changes in appearance or use.

Material composition matters as well. Different materials have different environmental impacts, and products containing more material generally have higher impacts, although the relationship varies by design and function. Using recycled content alone does not necessarily guarantee a lower overall impact. Material quantities, manufacturing processes, durability, and how long a product remains useful all influence its environmental performance. Designing with fewer unnecessary components, selecting appropriate materials, and making products easier to maintain can therefore help address the problem at its source.

Material quantities, manufacturing processes, durability, and how long a product remains useful all influence its environmental performance. Designing with fewer unnecessary components, selecting appropriate materials, and making products easier to maintain can therefore help address the problem at its source.

Products such as Boss Design's Lucy lounge chair provide an example of this approach. Developed within The Loop framework, Lucy features a fully removable upholstery cover that can be replaced on site. Rather than requiring the entire chair to be removed when the fabric needs a change, the design allows the upholstery to be renewed while retaining the existing structure. The chair also incorporates BioPUR® foam, a recyclable internal steel frame, responsibly sourced plywood, and minimal fixings intended to facilitate disassembly. These features address different aspects of material selection, maintenance, and recovery.

Keeping Existing Furniture in Circulation

Collections such as the Lucy lounge chair illustrate how repairability can be considered alongside comfort and appearance from the outset. Their actual environmental benefits depend on how the product is used and maintained, as well as whether components are ultimately renewed or recovered, which is why product design is only one part of the process. Even furniture designed for longevity may be discarded if owners lack the time, information, or services needed to maintain it. Extending its useful life therefore also requires practical ways to assess existing products and determine what should happen to them when a project changes.

Even furniture designed for longevity may be discarded if owners lack the time, information, or services needed to maintain it. Extending its useful life therefore also requires practical ways to assess existing products and determine what should happen to them when a project changes.

Efforts such as The Loop address several possibilities and opportunities. Its ReNew service supports repairing and reupholstering eligible furniture, while ReUse helps organizations redistribute existing pieces between departments, floors, or locations. ReSell provides a route to buy back selected furniture, renew it where necessary, and return it to use in future projects. Through RePurpose, furniture that no longer suits one setting can be redirected to charities, educational environments, and community projects. Recycling is considered when further use or renewal is not viable.

For architects, interior designers and owners, it is important to consider not only how furniture will perform in a completed space, but also how it might remain useful as that space changes. Also, before specifying new furniture for a refurbishment, assessing existing pieces can help identify what to retain, repair, adapt, or redistribute. Clear information on materials, maintenance requirements, and construction can make these decisions easier.

Reducing furniture waste requires attention to both the products being made and the systems through which they are purchased, maintained, and eventually discarded. Material selection and manufacturing efficiency remain important, but so does the ability to retain the resources already invested in an existing product.

#8970. Sharjah Design Centre Unveils Plans for Rammed Earth Building Opening in 2029

Sharjah Design Centre (SDC), a new institution dedicated to design, material research, prototyping, and production, is scheduled to open in 2029 as part of the Sharjah Creative Quarter in the United Arab Emirates. Designed by Taller de Arquitectura – Mauricio Rocha in collaboration with architect Daniel Rosselló, the centre will bring together specialist laboratories, research facilities, production spaces, and public programmes within a purpose-built building. Under the leadership of H.E. Sheikha Hind bint Majid Al Qasimi, SDC aims to connect designers, manufacturers, researchers, and entrepreneurs through an integrated framework for material experimentation, fabrication, and knowledge exchange.

Sharjah Design Centre (SDC), a new institution dedicated to design, material research, prototyping, and production, is scheduled to open in 2029 as part of the Sharjah Creative Quarter in the United Arab Emirates. Designed by Taller de Arquitectura – Mauricio Rocha in collaboration with architect Daniel Rosselló, the centre will bring together specialist laboratories, research facilities, production spaces, and public programmes within a purpose-built building. Under the leadership of H.E. Sheikha Hind bint Majid Al Qasimi, SDC aims to connect designers, manufacturers, researchers, and entrepreneurs through an integrated framework for material experimentation, fabrication, and knowledge exchange.

The building's architecture responds to the local climate and landscape through the integration of local materials, vernacular principles, and contemporary technology. Rammed earth construction is incorporated into the design as part of an approach to reducing environmental impact. As a component of the Sharjah Creative Quarter, SDC will join institutions including Irthi Museum, Sharjah Fashion Lab, Qasimi Archives, the Sheikha Jawaher bint Mohammed Al Qasimi Collection, and L'ÉCOLE, School of Jewelry Arts, supported by Van Cleef & Arpels. The district is scheduled to open in 2029, bringing together cultural, educational, and creative institutions within a shared urban setting.

The district is scheduled to open in 2029, bringing together cultural, educational, and creative institutions within a shared urban setting.

Located across from Sharjah's University City and adjacent to the House of Wisdom, the centre will form part of a newly established cultural district dedicated to art, design, craft, fashion, and cultural heritage. The Sharjah Creative Quarter is conceived as an interconnected network of institutions supporting creative industries through research, education, production, and public engagement. Within this framework, SDC will focus on connecting design research with manufacturing capabilities and professional practice, providing infrastructure for the development of projects from initial experimentation to material application.

The centre's facilities will include seven specialist laboratories dedicated to textiles, rapid prototyping, glass, ceramics, jewellery, metal, and wood, alongside a Material Library, Digital Archive, exhibition spaces, co-working areas, private studios, and a retail space. The Material Library will catalogue material research, document experimental materials, and support education through a collection of design-related publications. Connected to the library, the Digital Archive will store research, digital publications, and industrial mappings, providing a searchable resource for the centre's members and researchers. SDC will also organise workshops, courses, masterclasses, residencies, collaborative research projects, and professional development programmes. These activities will address the relationship between design education and professional practice while facilitating collaboration between designers and industry.

SDC will also organise workshops, courses, masterclasses, residencies, collaborative research projects, and professional development programmes. These activities will address the relationship between design education and professional practice while facilitating collaboration between designers and industry.

Research collaborations are already underway with Atelier LUMA, a programme of LUMA Arles, and the American University of Sharjah (AUS), focusing on local material research and potential applications. The work is supported by the AUS Energy, Water, and Sustainable Environment Research Center, BEEAH, and Sharjah National Oil Corporation. Through Theatrum Al Kimiya, an ongoing research initiative developed with Atelier LUMA, SDC is investigating locally sourced and waste-based materials, including salt, brine, limestone, sand, clay, palm, shells, demolition waste, ceramic waste, wool, and mycelium. The research builds on Irthi Contemporary Crafts Council's Architecture of Culture publication, released in 2023, translating material research findings from craft into design applications.

#8969. 3 Signs You’re the ‘Fringe Friend’ of Your Group, According to a Psychologist

Welcome to Asking for a Friend, a weekly series dedicated to solving the messy, awkward, and confusing parts of modern friendship. Because the truth is, our platonic relationships are often the most complicated. Send us your friendship dilemmas here, and we might feature one in a future column.

Technically, you’re part of a friend group…well, loosely speaking. You’re in the chats. You receive the invites, but usually ones that sound like “Oh, but you can come if you want”...which, the more you think of it, lands less like inclusion and more like a pity afterthought.

You’re there for big, public-facing plans—birthday parties, girls’ trips, anything that benefits from a larger headcount—yet absent from spontaneous happy hours and nights out where real bonding happens and the inside jokes are born.

If any of this hits close to home, you might be what some people call the backup or “fringe friend.”

We can’t all be everyone’s number one. But what makes this situation so hard is that there’s no obvious villain and no dramatic fallout (which, in some ways, would almost be easier to deal with). Instead, you’re left with a low-grade, hard-to-prove insecurity: Am I just…no one’s first choice? I’m their friend…but are they mine?

For this week’s column, SELF tapped Christina Ferrari, PsyD, a Miami-based psychologist to break down three clear signs you’re a second-tier “backup friend.”

As in, you hear about each plan the day of. You’re added to existing dinner reservations only after somebody else has cancelled. Of course, this might be a matter of logistics or innocent forgetfulness, which is why “every now and then, it’s not cause for concern,” Dr. Ferrari tells SELF. People who are disorganized across the board also exist. “So if this is how they are with all of their friends, that might reflect more about their poor planning”—annoying in its own way, but ultimately a separate issue. The point is, pay attention to the pattern if you can recall more than a few instances.

A few of these tells are subtle yet revealing. Somehow, get-togethers conveniently skip the messy, in-between stage of coordination (“Does 7 work?” “Where should we go?”), arriving at you fully formed. Or, in person, everyone references memes, messages, or memories that clearly happened…just not in any chat you’re in.

“It's totally normal for people to have multiple friendships and separate interactions,” Dr. Ferrari points out. “This isn’t about being included in everything.” Still, paying attention to how often this occurs makes it easier to understand “why you feel like you’re constantly stepping into something already established rather than being part of it from the beginning,” Dr. Ferrari explains.

“Life, of course, can get busy, and a temporary imbalance is normal,” Dr. Ferrari says. But when you’re truly in the crew, your absence will be missed or, at the very least, acknowledged. Someone will notice: “Wait, where have you been?” “I haven’t seen you in forever.” “We never see you anymore.” “Let’s catch up.”

There’s usually, in other words, a small moment of recognition—an indication that you exist in their shared awareness when you’re not physically present, which is why when you don’t get any of those little check-ins, it’s disorienting. It’s as if you’re not important enough to be missed.

Bring it up, and you risk sounding insecure. Say nothing, and you’ll continue to overanalyze every delayed invite, every inside joke, and every Instagram story you weren’t tagged in.

None of the options above sounds appealing. Though if you do want to say something, Dr. Ferrari recommends a low-pressure check-in like: “I always have such a great time when we all hang out. Next time, I'd love to be looped in!” It’s warm, subtle, and assumes good intent—the kind of communication that makes your intentions clear without putting anyone on the defensive. But in ambiguous situations like these—where your gut is whispering that something’s off, yet no one is technically doing you wrong—even the most carefully crafted messages can’t give you the reassurance (or confidence) you’re seeking.

That’s why the solution isn’t necessarily, “How do I become a core member of this group?” Dr. Ferrari says, but instead: “Am I spending my energy where I actually feel like I matter?”

Nobody deserves to feel disposable with people they care about most. And it’s worth remembering that not being fully “in” in one circle doesn’t mean you’re inherently less than, which is where a different solution comes in: Expand your social network instead of over-investing in your current one.

In other words, go out of your comfort zone and start weekly lunches with your favorite coworker. Finally say yes to that old high school companion you’ve been meaning to reach out to but haven’t prioritized. Agree to that weekend trip with friends-of-friends instead of defaulting to your usual group or staying in.

Sometimes, all it takes is noticing the spaces where you’re truly welcome to ease the ache of feeling like the “unimportant” one.
