Let's make this concrete. You're flying into Nashville for a long weekend — maybe it's a bachelorette party, a music festival, or just a trip you've been putting off. You pull up Hyatt.com and search Nashville for a Friday–Sunday stay (two nights).

The Hyatt Place Nashville / Brentwood shows cash rates of $169 per night — that's $338 for your two-night stay before taxes. Totally reasonable for Nashville on a weekend, but $338 is $338.

Now look at the award column: 5,000 points per night. Two nights: 10,000 points.

You transferred 10,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards points from your Sapphire Reserve to World of Hyatt last week (it took about 30 seconds, and at 1:1 every point landed). Your Hyatt account shows a 10,000-point balance. You complete the booking, pay the ~$30 in taxes at checkout, and you're done.

That's more than three times the value most people extract from their points programs. And those 10,000 Chase UR points? You earned them by putting your regular monthly spending on your Chase Sapphire card for a few months.

At the Hyatt Place, you'll check into a well-appointed room with a king bed, a sofa sleating area, and a bathroom that doesn't make you feel like you're in a budget motel. Hyatt House properties (also frequently Category 1 or 2) often include a complimentary hot breakfast — eggs, waffles, fruit — served every morning. In some suburban markets, these properties also offer free parking, turning your 5,000-point night into an even stronger value play when you factor in parking rates that might otherwise run $20–$30/night.

This isn't a flashy Park Hyatt penthouse suite. But it's a genuinely comfortable, predictably high-quality stay that you've effectively taken off your cash budget — freeing that $338 for experiences, food, or your investment accounts. That's the ChooseFI mindset applied to travel.

Stack your Hyatt Globalist benefits if you qualify. If you hold World of Hyatt's top elite status (Globalist, earned at 60 qualifying nights), you receive complimentary breakfast at most full-service properties and room upgrades. Even on a 5,000-point award night, your elite benefits apply. That free breakfast alone can add $25–$35 of value to every morning.

Use the Hyatt free night award from the World of Hyatt Credit Card. The World of Hyatt Credit Card (issued by Chase) comes with an annual free night certificate valid at Category 1–4 properties. Stack this with a paid or points night to effectively get one night free on a multi-night stay — no points required.

Book as far out as you can. The Hyatt booking window opens 395 days in advance. For peak travel periods — summer weekends, holiday weekends, major events — inventory at Category 1 properties can thin out. Getting in early locks your room and your rate.

Target Hyatt House properties for family trips. Hyatt House locations frequently feature suite-style rooms with full kitchens, separate living areas, and free hot breakfast included for all guests. A family of four can stay comfortably for 5,000–8,000 points and skip the cost of restaurant breakfasts entirely.

Earn points on the Bilt card on Rent Day. Bilt Rewards runs a bonus promotion on the first of each month — transferring points earned that day at elevated rates. Accumulating Bilt points through rent payments (no transaction fee) is one of the most efficient ways to build a Hyatt balance.

Don't transfer points speculatively. Even though Chase and Bilt transfers to Hyatt are instant, always confirm your specific dates show award availability before transferring. Points transferred to Hyatt cannot be moved back.

Don't ignore the expiration policy. World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of account inactivity. A single qualifying activity — a points transfer, a stay, a credit card purchase — resets the clock. Set a calendar reminder annually to ensure you don't lose your balance.

Don't overlook Category 2 properties. At 8,000 points per night, Category 2 Hyatts often include urban full-service hotels that provide dramatically more value than the jump in points cost suggests. Once you're comfortable with Category 1 redemptions, explore Category 2 as a natural next step.

This redemption was built for the travel rewards beginner — the person who has accumulated their first 10,000–20,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards or Bilt points and isn't yet sure if the whole system is real. It's also for the seasoned optimizer who wants a reliable, low-friction redemption they can execute on short notice.

Minimum points needed: 5,000 for a single night. Most people engaging seriously with Chase UR earning will accumulate this through normal spending in a single billing cycle.

In the broader ChooseFI travel strategy, Category 1 Hyatt nights serve as the building blocks — the reliable, repeatable foundation that funds your domestic travel while you accumulate larger balances for the aspirational redemptions.

**Difficulty Rating: Easy — and we mean it.** This is the redemption we'd hand to someone who just got their first travel rewards credit card and wants to see if the points are real. The score of 5/5 on Beginner Friendliness reflects every dimension of the experience: earning the points is straightforward, the transfer path is clear, the booking interface is clean, and availability is abundant. **What makes this easy:** - **No complex routing rules.** There's no geographic zone logic, no partner airline ticketing, no stopover rules to navigate. You pick a hotel, check availability, transfer points, and book. That's the entire process. - **Instant transfers.** Both Chase Ultimate Rewards and Bilt Rewards transfer to World of Hyatt instantly. You can go from zero Hyatt points to a confirmed reservation in under five minutes. - **Reliable availability.** Category 1 properties are upper-midscale hotels with large room inventories. Award availability is rarely the bottleneck at this tier. **The one thing to watch:** Points don't live in Hyatt until you transfer them — and they can't come back once transferred. Always search hyatt.com *first*, confirm your dates show award space, *then* transfer. This single habit eliminates the only real risk in the process. **Tips for first-timers:** 1. Create your free World of Hyatt account before you need it — having your membership number ready speeds the transfer process. 2. Start with a one-night stay to build confidence, then scale up. 3. Screenshot your confirmation email and points balance after booking — it feels good, and it's good record-keeping. If you've ever booked a hotel room online, you can execute this redemption. Go do it.

Category 1 primarily includes Hyatt Place and Hyatt House properties in secondary markets, smaller cities, and suburban locations. These are upper-midscale hotels with consistently good quality — clean rooms, modern decor, and amenities like free Wi-Fi. Hyatt House properties often include complimentary breakfast and kitchen suites.

Yes. Chase Ultimate Rewards transfer to World of Hyatt instantly — at 1:1 with a Sapphire Reserve and 4:3 with a Sapphire Preferred (4 UR points = 3 Hyatt points). You need a Chase Sapphire Preferred, Sapphire Reserve, or Ink Business Preferred to access transfer partners. The Chase Freedom Unlimited and Freedom Flex can pool points into a Sapphire account for transfers.

Yes. Because Hyatt uses a fixed award chart, Category 1 properties cost 5,000 points per night regardless of the day of the week or season. However, award availability itself can vary — popular properties during high-demand weekends may show no award availability even though the price remains 5,000 points when rooms are available.

At 5,000 points for a $100 to $200 room, you are getting 2 to 4 cents per point — two to four times the value of redeeming the same Chase Ultimate Rewards points as 1 cent per point cash back. Even compared to the Sapphire Reserve portal rate of 1.5 cents per point, Category 1 Hyatt bookings consistently deliver superior value. Note that Sapphire Preferred holders transfer at 4:3, so factor in the conversion when comparing.

Category 1 Hyatt hotels are the single best entry point into travel rewards for the FI community. At 5,000 points per night with cash values of $100 to $200, you consistently achieve 2 to 4 cents per point — a redemption rate that proves the system works before you ever attempt a complex international booking. Transfer points instantly from Chase Ultimate Rewards (1:1 via Sapphire Reserve, 4:3 via Sapphire Preferred) or Bilt (1:1), book directly through Hyatt, and pay only taxes at checkout. This is the foundational redemption that builds your travel rewards confidence and conviction.

#8913. Can’t get back into working out? It’s not a motivation problem.

Recently, I asked you: where are you feeling most stuck with your fitness right now?

Hundreds of you wrote back. Thoughtful, honest answers. Thank you.

And one theme jumped out at me IMMEDIATELY.

One reader, let’s call her Supergirl, said it this way:

If you’ve ever had a great run (for a few days or a few years) and then couldn’t find your way back, this one’s for you, too.

I’ve heard this so many times in my coaching career. You were in a really good groove. Something knocked you off. And getting back on track feels incredibly difficult, and you don’t know why.

I’ve experienced this myself! I was in a groove with food logging. It felt easy. Then I took a break, and when I tried to start up again, I couldn’t get it going with any consistency for the life of me.

Here’s my take after nearly two decades of coaching: I doubt this is a motivation thing.

You were cruising at 70 miles an hour. You made a pit stop, and now you’re trying to jump the car straight back to 70. Instantly.

Another reader put it really well in their message to me:

That’s driving with your eyes on the rearview mirror. And it makes anything smaller feel like it doesn’t count.

But smaller is how you get back up to speed.

After multiple false starts with food logging, I realized I was falling into the same trap. And instead of forcing myself to weigh and measure anything, I gave myself a different on-ramp. Protein and veggies at each meal? Check. That allowed me to build back up again and find the groove that worked for me in this current phase of life.

Previous success can feel like a scorecard that you have to grade yourself against.

But what worked before might not work for you right now.

And it’s important to remember that most of us needed an on-ramp the first time, too. That part didn’t change after some time off.

You know what you “should” be doing. Let’s put that aside for now.

Instead, let’s shrink down what our focus is. We don’t have to figure out the whole routine. Not the whole week. Let’s work on today.

Try this thought experiment with me: if you didn’t have any expectations of what this “should” look like, what is one thing that feels doable today?

Maybe it’s performing your warm-up routine. Or doing the first round of exercises in your workout.

Maybe it’s batch cooking some protein tonight, or running to the grocery store to stock up on some easy fruit and veggie options.

Try it out, and see how that feels. Is the resistance still there? If it isn’t, you’ve found the start of your on-ramp. 🙌

And if it still feels hard to start? That’s OK, too. We can choose a different entry point and try again.

If you’re in that camp of “I know what to do. I can’t get myself to start,” give yourself a different, smaller on-ramp.

But it may be exactly what you need right now.

Hit reply and let me know what yours looks like.

Nerd Fitness cuts through the fitness B.S. to help people get stronger, healthier, and more confident – all with a fun, no-nonsense approach.

#8911. Camel Pose Helps Build Balance, Strength, and Flexibility

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about Camel Pose first appeared in the September-October 2001 issue of Yoga Journal. You can find more of our Archives here.

When looking at the meanings of the names of yoga asanas, especially those named after animals, you can find clues—sometimes literal and other times only suggestive —about the nature of the pose. With Camel Pose (Ustrasana) it’s a little of both.

What was it about this pose that inspired yogis of ages past to name it after the camel? Only by strenuously stretching the imagination can we find any resemblance to a healthy backbend in the shape of this animal.

Anatomically a camel’s body appears to be an assemblage of odd, unrelated parts, and the hump—the most unique and obvious characteristic—looks almost like an afterthought. Although camel humps may appear to be part of the spine, they are actually sacks of fat used to store partially digested food for long journeys. Through centuries of Asian and African civilization, the camel has also had a reputation for being a stubborn, ill-tempered animal with a serious lack of intelligence. Since it’s doubtful that the ancient yogis aspired to the image of lifting the spine like a camel hump, and a camel’s temperament is not exactly something to emulate in one’s yoga practice, why is this posed called the “camel”?

Traditionally the camel’s presence in the desert, one of the most inhospitable environments on our planet, has been one of the primary forces sustaining human life there. Though a camel’s eyesight is not keen, it relies on some inner compass to navigate its way through the desert. Used primarily as pack animals, camels instinctively know if a load is too heavy to endure over a long journey or if the weight is improperly balanced —and will refuse to move until the load is adjusted. Without a road map, in constantly changing surroundings of drifting sands, camels have the ability to read the signs and find the oases of green where water is present and food at hand.

Looking at the Camel Pose, we can begin to see a parallel. For many beginners, the “environment” in backbends is equally inhospitable. In general, beginning to bend backward is difficult and sometimes frightening, yet backbends are essential to maintaining a healthy spine. Generally we function in a forward-facing, right-side-up world, relying heavily on our eyes for our sense of identity and direction. In Camel, we must learn to cultivate another way of seeing. The shape of the pose places the head and one’s vision behind the body. It is an alien experience; our view of the world is literally turned upside down.

Our normal context for relating to ourselves and the image that sustains us is lost. For the beginner, a common reaction to the fear that comes from this loss of context is to shorten or hold the breath.

In addition, beginners often habitually contract the muscles of the buttocks and abdomen. The neck, if weak, becomes vulnerable as the shoulders grip for protection. When these reactions are present in the body, the movement in this pose does not respond well, especially if the student uses excessive muscular force. The pose feels out of balance, and the more we struggle, the less the pose responds. This only deepens the frustration, and we are likely to shut down or check out.

Basically there are two techniques for entering Camel Pose safely: dropping in from an upright kneeling position or lifting up from a seated position. Once you master these approaches in Camel Pose, a foundation has been laid for approaching the more advanced backbend Wheel Pose (Urdhva Dhanurasana) either by lifting up from the floor or by dropping back from a standing position.

I recommend dropping in from the kneeling position in Camel for your first attempt if your lower back or knees are sensitive. This approach also works with gravity to help you avoid the natural tendencies of the beginner to overdo muscular effort. Begin by kneeling on your mat with your torso upright and the thighs perpendicular to the floor. Place your legs hip-width apart, with the tops of the feet flat on the floor and your arms at your sides. If your lower back is weak, place your hands on your buttocks to give more support to the lumbar spine as you enter the pose. Let your shoulders hang from the sides of your neck and drop your collarbones away from your ears. Initially keep your head upright, with your chin drawn slightly in toward the center of the throat. As you inhale, feel the fullness of your breath feeding the back, rather than the chest.

With each exhalation, let the weight of your chest and abdominal organs sink, as you keep the spine engaged upward from the back of the skull. Visualize the energy of the pose looping down along the front of the body (from the chest down through the hips to the shinbones on the floor) and up along the back of the body (through the spine to the crown of the head). Slowly take your head back; keep the throat soft and the shoulders down and slightly forward, with the shoulder blades broad. Avoid hardening the buttocks or the abdomen. Keep the top of the hips pressing firmly down into the knees, and as you bend the spine backward, let your arms hang from your shoulders with your fingers reaching back to touch the heels.

If the stress is excessive in your lower back, inhale back to an upright position, and after resting for a moment, try the pose again. Once your hands reach your feet, maintain the downward pressure from the top of the hip bones pressing into the knees, continue releasing the chest and abdomen down, and feel the lift from the floor into the thoracic spine.

The head should hang freely, with the neck supported by the width of the trapezius muscle along the top of the shoulders. The breath should remain slow and rhythmic, and with each exhalation, the release of the frontal body will propel the lift in the back body. After three or four cycles of breath, inhale back to an upright position.

Lifting up from the seated position can be more accessible when the neck is weak, but it tends to stress the legs and knees more intensely than the first approach, due to the fact that you are working against gravity. If your knees are weak, take care not to overstress them. And be patient—if your knees and groins are tight, you may not achieve full extension in the pose at first.

From an upright kneeling position, sit between your heels (use a block between your feet if necessary, with the palms of your hands placed on your heels, fingers pointing back. Slowly lean back, straightening your arms, taking your weight onto your hands, and lift your hips upward.

Press the shoulders forward, broaden the shoulder blades, and let the neck rest in the trapezius muscle as you take the head slowly back. As the hips lift upward and more weight is taken onto the lower legs, press the tops of the hip bones (ilia) down into the knees and lift the spine. Be careful to keep the abdomen and buttocks soft and the energy of the chest dropping.

Once you are in the pose, the release of the frontal body will propel the lift in the back body. After three or four cycles of breath, slowly lower your hips on an inhalation and return to the seated position. With Camel Pose, you begin to develop balance and strength in the spine, promoting flexibility in the shoulders and suppleness in the abdomen. By relying less on outer sight for your sense of identity and position in the world, you can cultivate an inner vision that expands into your more authentic, intuitive self.

#8910. Transform Your Core with This 10-Minute Exercise Ball Workout

An exercise (or stability) ball is an inexpensive but effective strength training tool for triathletes. (Photo: Getty Images)

For this article, retired pro triathlete and Triathlete contributor Emma-Kate Lidbury spoke to strength coach and former pro Dede Griesbauer about why this stability ball workout is so effective for triathletes.

Here’s the thing about strength training for triathletes: Almost nobody skips it because they don’t believe in it. They skip it because of the drive to the gym or the 90 minutes that don’t exist between that threshold bike workout and school pickup.

So what if we make life a little easier and remove some of the barriers to getting strength done?

This routine does exactly that and requires one piece of equipment – an exercise ball – and a patch of floor about the size of a yoga mat. No need for dumbbells, a bench, a gym membership, or the drive there. You can pick up an exercise ball for about the same price as a mid-range pair of goggles; it can fit into most any suitcase; and it might just help you find every stabilizer muscle you’ve quietly neglected since your last off-season strength block.

A stability ball is, by design, unstable. That’s the entire value proposition. It offers the following benefits:

Every exercise here demands you hold a neutral spine against something actively trying to move you out of it. Former pro triathlete turned strength coach Dede Griesbauer points out that this pays off in two places triathletes care about: run efficiency, and the ability to hold a stable position in the aerobars.

With an exercise like the rear foot elevated lunge (below), Griesbauer notes this forces each leg to work independently, which may reveal the left-right discrepancies a bilateral squat lets you hide. This matters for power balance on the bike and for not favoring one side on the run, which can help reduce injury risk.

Almost every movement in this routine trains multiple muscle groups at once. Griesbauer’s summary: It offers good “bang for the buck” with minimal equipment, minimal space, and minimal setup.

Griesbauer advises adding strength work to your hard days, not because it’s pleasant to stack lifting onto a threshold run, but because the alternative – sprinkling it across easy days – erodes the recovery that those days are designed to deliver.

“Make your hard days hard so that your easy days can be easy,” she says.

That’s the ideal. Griesbauer is also clear about what “ideal” might look like for an age-grouper with a job.

“Not everyone will have time to do their hard bike or run session AND make time for strength on the same day,” she says. “The good news is that this session isn’t heavy loading. These are good basic movements, so if you are time-crunched, adding them wherever you can is better than not doing them at all.”

Two sessions a week is the target, but once isn’t a failure. “Some is better than none,” Griesbauer says, “so if you can only do it once? Get it done once.”

Start with a single pass through all nine exercises (which should take approximately 10-12 minutes).

Once one round stops feeling like work, add a second. Then, if time allows, add a third. Three circuits should take you about 30-35 minutes and is plenty of stimulus for a routine that isn’t loading you heavily. Rest 30 to 60 seconds between exercises and a couple of minutes between rounds.

Progress through the workout in the order listed. It moves between lower body, core, and upper body so nothing fatigues to failure.

Stand on your right foot with your left leg extended behind you and the top of your left foot resting on the ball. Bend your right knee until your right thigh is parallel to the floor, keeping your torso upright and your weight on your heel. Now press your heel into the floor and return to the start position. Complete 10 repetitions and then repeat the exercise with your left leg.

Begin in a prone position with the tops of your feet resting on the ball, your palms on the floor underneath your shoulders, and your body forming a straight line. Now contract your stomach muscles, bend your knees, and roll the ball toward your chest. Pause briefly and roll the ball back until your body forms a straight line again. Complete 12 repetitions.

Assume a modified push-up position with your feet together, your body forming a perfectly straight line and your palms positioned slightly more than shoulder-width apart on the ball. Bend your elbows and smoothly lower your chest to within an inch of the ball. Immediately press back upward to the start position. If you have difficulty doing a full push-up, do a half push-up, bending your elbows only to 90 degrees before pressing upward. Complete 10 repetitions.

Start in a bridge position, face up, with your head and shoulders on the floor and your heels resting on top of the ball, your body suspended in a straight line between these points. Contract your hamstrings and roll the ball toward your butt. Pause briefly and extend your legs, rolling the ball back to the starting point. Don’t let your hips drop. Complete 12 repetitions. If this exercise is too easy, do a single-leg version, elevating one foot above the ball and pulling the ball toward your butt with the other leg.

Kneel on the floor facing the ball, lean forward slightly, and place your forearms on top of the ball. Pull your belly button toward your spine. Slowly roll the ball forward by extending your forearms out in front of you and allowing your body to tilt toward the floor. Concentrate on maintaining perfect alignment of your spine. Stop just before you’re forced to arch your back. Hold this position for a two-count and then return to the start position, exhaling as you do so. Complete 12 repetitions.

Lie facedown on the ball with your palms on the floor. Begin with the ball supporting your pelvic area. Now use your hands to drag your body forward over the ball until it is underneath the tops of your feet, keeping your body in a straight line. Pause briefly and roll back to the start position. Complete 10 repetitions.

Assume a modified push-up position with your palms on the floor, the tops of your feet resting on the ball, and your body in a perfectly straight line between them. Bend your elbows and lower your chest toward the floor. Go as far as you can without strain; it’s OK if it isn’t very far. Now press back to the start position. Complete 10 repetitions.

Lie face up with your upper back supported by the ball, your feet flat on the floor about 12 inches apart, your knees bent and your body forming a “tabletop” from knees to chest. Contract your calf muscles and raise your heels off the floor without allowing your hips to sag. Now lower your heels back to the floor. Complete 12 repetitions. If this exercise is too easy, do a single-leg version, first crossing your left ankle over your right knee and then doing the reverse.

Get into a plank position with your palms on the floor underneath your chest and the ball supporting your shins. Keeping your arms straight, press the heels of your palms into the floor and push your body backward so that the ball rolls up under your thighs. Go as far as you can and then pull your body in the opposite direction until you’re back in the start position. Complete 12 repetitions. If this exercise is too easy, start with the ball under the tops of your feet.

Instability is the point, which also means this routine isn’t universally appropriate. Griesbauer flags a few pointers worth knowing before you start. Note that none of these are a reason not to train. They just require you to adapt or swap movements if needed.

If you have a cranky lower back: The abdominal rollout generates high spinal extension and shear force if your core gives out mid-rep, which can be a genuine problem for anyone with disc history. The reverse crunch can pull you into loaded lumbar flexion if control slips, and a hamstring curl performed with dropped hips will arch and cramp the low back.

If you have “shoulder history”: Push-ups on a moving ball tax the rotator cuff hard, and the ball walk-out places prolonged, shifting load on the shoulder joint. Skip both if you’ve dealt with instability or impingement.

If you have wrist issues: The ball’s spherical surface forces the wrists into deep extension while the weight moves under you. Elevated push-ups shift more bodyweight forward onto the same joints.

If you have knees and hip flexor problems: The rear foot elevated lunge loads the front knee in deep flexion and stretches the trailing leg aggressively, which can be enough to tip the pelvis if your hip flexors are tight. Tight hip flexors will also hijack the reverse crunch from the lower abs.

If you have cramp-prone calves and hamstrings: The bridge heel raise fires the calves while the hamstrings are already shortened, which is a reliable spasm trigger. The hamstring curl frequently cramps athletes with weak hamstrings on the concentric.

If you have compromised balance: Any single-leg work raises fall risk. Have a wall or chair within reach if you feel you might need it.

#8909. Inside an Elite Running Group’s Marathon Training Strategies That Get Them to the Front of the Pack

Go inside the Boulder-based team helping Hellen Obiri, Joe Klecker, and others chase NYC success, and learn how their approach can improve your own training.

Six years ago, when Joe Klecker was named to the inaugural class of the On Athletics Club (OAC) in Boulder, Colorado, his goals were all about racing fast on the track. But based on his physiology, his tenacity, and even his genes, coach Dathan Ritzenhein already knew Klecker was destined to become a marathoner—and probably a very good one.

When the team now known as OAC Global formed in the summer of 2020, it featured eight postcollegiate runners chasing Olympic berths from 1,500 to 10,000 meters. The OAC sent several runners (including Klecker) to the Tokyo Olympics and brought home medals from Paris.

But track success was only the first step of what Ritzenhein envisioned. In the years since, he and coach Laura Thweatt have built an elite marathon program, too.

Kenyan great Hellen Obiri, four-time Major Marathon winner and current women’s New York City Marathon course record holder, put OAC on the marathon map after joining in 2022. The progression of Klecker (with a marathon PR of 2:05:56 from Boston), along with newer teammates Ryan Ford (2:05:46 marathon PR) and Patrick Kiprop (59:14 half marathon PR), has helped to solidify the team’s presence on the roads.

As all four prepare for the NYC Marathon, we went behind the curtain at the OAC Global Training Facility in Boulder to learn what has fueled their success.

When On recruited Obiri to Boulder in 2022, the two-time Olympic silver medalist at 5,000 meters was about to move up to the marathon. That meant shifting from pure track speed and relatively low mileage (80 miles per week) to 120- to 125-mile weeks and grinding sessions like 25K tempo runs.

With no other marathoners on the team, she did portions of her long runs with 10,000-meter runner Alicia Monson and some longer tempo efforts and fartleks with Klecker. All three benefited.

Obiri became one of the best marathoners in the world, winning New York and Boston twice and an Olympic bronze medal in Paris; Monson broke the American 5,000- and 10,000-meter records in 2023, and Klecker got a taste of what marathon training was all about, which gave him proper perspective as he was about to begin his first marathon build.

“[Obiri’s] level is so high that, on a lot of our long runs and even some fartleks, we would overlap for a good chunk of those workouts,” Klecker, 29, tells Runner’s World. “And for me, it was harder than I thought. When you’re racing on the track, a long run is kind of a chill day because all of your hard work is on the track. But when you’d see her go out and do her long runs, she was just hammering from the start, and so I knew I really had to wrap my head around this new way of training for the roads.”

As Klecker got closer to his marathon debut last fall, the OAC signed Ford as his primary training partner. They developed a synergy, but weren’t entirely aligned in their schedules because Ford was building up to the Chicago Marathon and Klecker was preparing for New York a month later. But they did sync up for all of their training (including harder workouts) as they prepared for Boston, and that paid off with better racing execution and significant time drops.

The team recently added an even faster teammate in Kiprop, a 25-year-old Kenyan and former University of Arkansas star, after big wins at the Lilac Bloomsday 12K and Peachtree Road Race 10K. He ran 59:14 in his half marathon debut in January in Houston and moved to Boulder in early August to join Klecker and Ford at the start of the 12-week New York buildup.

Klecker admits his marathon debut was mostly about surviving 26 miles. He trained to run a measured race holding 5:00 pace the whole way. That meant he fell off the lead pack when surging began along First Avenue, but his strength allowed him to reel in runners who were fading in the final miles.

This year, the trio of Klecker, Ford, and Kiprop have been able to push each other on hard long runs and marathon-specific workouts aimed at mimicking the surges and inconsistent pacing at the front of the pack in New York City.

“This year, the goal is to be up front and try to race for that podium and not just catch the people who die. You can’t do that from two minutes back late in the race,” Klecker says. “Now, based on the training we’ve done through a natural progression of workouts, it feels I should be ready to go with some moves. That's kind of been the whole focus of the past year, to be more competitive throughout the race.”

Training with the team has worked well for Obiri, 36, who is coming off a personal best 2:15:53 runner-up effort at the London Marathon in April. But at times, she has had a penchant to run too hard in training with faster teammates, which is why OAC has recruited seasonal training partners closer to her pace from Kenya over the past two years. (This year, it is Dennis Kipkosgeu, a 2:13 marathoner.)

She heads to New York as the defending champion after what she considers her best buildup yet.

“The growth of our road running team feels amazing because I have runners to train with every day,” she says of the OAC team. “When I joined in 2022, I was the only marathoner, and that was hard. This gives me confidence because there are four of us working so hard together.”

By early 2025, Ritzenhein wanted a coach to lead the road program day to day while he and assistant coach Kelsey Quinn stayed focused on the track group that included Yared Nuguse, bronze medalist in the 1500 at the Paris Olympics.

Thweatt, a longtime Boulder runner, had just retired from her own pro career and posted on Instagram that she was looking for new opportunities. Two days later, Ritzenhein called her. Within about two weeks, she was the OAC’s marathon coach.

A 2:25:38 marathoner who twice finished fifth at the U.S. Olympic Trials (in the marathon in 2020 and 10,000 meters in 2016) and notched top-10 finishes in London and New York, Thweatt admits she initially wasn’t sure what she could offer runners much faster than her. But early in the New York build, she ran with Obiri several days a week; as the workouts got faster, she paced her from a bike.

Thweatt quickly learned the role of a coach is more than just explaining and monitoring workouts and more about sharing experiences, reducing stressors, instilling confidence, visualizing race-day situations, keeping athletes focused on the process, and making sure they run easy enough on their easy days—all key elements of marathon training.

The runners are doing the work in training, but a coach is the glue that brings it all together, Thweatt says, and that’s true for any level of runner.

Kiprop says he has relied on the experience of his coaches and teammates during this first marathon build, so much so that he believes his entry into racing 26.2 miles might be easier than most. He heads to New York with a new level of fitness and plenty of firsthand course knowledge and pre-race logistics from Klecker, Obiri, Ford, Thweatt, and Ritzenhein, who all ran their first marathons on the five-borough course.

“At first, I didn’t know if I could handle the training for the marathon,” he says. “But with time, as you train together, you build that confidence, you build the courage to face the marathon.”

Ritzenhein signed on as the OAC’s first coach just weeks after his last pro race in early 2020, eager to build a program that would span more than a single Olympic cycle. He knew that would require patience, a supportive team atmosphere, and top-tier facilities.

Today, the OAC Global roster has 20 athletes from eight countries and operates out of its own 10,000-square-foot training center eight miles north of downtown Boulder, opened in 2024. It’s the nerve center for everything the team does: training, fueling, strength work, and communications. But it also serves as a place to develop camaraderie and team chemistry, which can help athletes thrive in a marathon training block, instead of just surviving.

“I think coming up with this facility was a genius idea,” Kiprop says. “It has everything we need. It’s nice to have your team around you here. When we’re together, it feels like family.”

The facility has two antigravity treadmills, eight Woodway treadmills, an underwater treadmill, and e-stim machines—most of which they use when there’s inclement weather and for rehab. There are treatment tables for massage therapists and physiotherapists, meeting space for sessions with coaches, dietitians, and mental strength counselors, and a lounge with a mini kitchen stocked with drinks, snacks, and supplements.

They also have a full gym with space for strength training, drills, and strides, an important part of their training, as marathon preparation is more than just running for the OAC crew. The team’s strength coaches, Jason Ross and Joslynn Peterson, have the runners do a wide range of running-specific and general strength exercises twice a week.

Most of the strength workouts focus on tissue health with longer isometrics (holding an exercise in one position as you would in a plank) at the beginning of a training cycle and then progress to increased weight and fewer reps, Ross tells Runner’s World. While each athlete has individual exercises to tackle, some of the common strength moves include weighted box step-ups, single-leg bent-knee hamstring isometric holds, trap bar deadlifts, landmine single-leg Romanian deadlifts, seated calf raises, and weighted standing calf raise isometrics.

“You cannot be complacent on that side of things,” Thweatt says. “It makes a huge difference. It’s an equal part of training. You need to make sure that everyone’s staying healthy and strong.”

Working alongside sports dietitians, each OAC marathoner has dialed in an individual fueling plan based on sweat testing and data from training. They know how many calories they burn on their long runs and hardest sessions, how much fluid and sodium they lose in their sweat, and exactly what they need to replace during a long run or hard session so they finish strong instead of fading late.

The exact details of what each runner needs are slightly different, Thweatt says, but they’re adept at consuming gels on the run and have practiced grabbing bottles off of tables, so they know how long they need to carry them and drink from them for optimal fueling.

“Fueling is one of the biggest things we drive home during training,” Thweatt says. “We’ve gone through the fueling plan in almost every training session that we do and we practice it like it’s going to be on race day. They know what’s going into their bottles on race day, so hopefully when we get to race day, it’s not even something they really have to think about because it’s what they’ve been doing for the last 12 weeks.”

While most runners prepare for marathons on a seven-day cycle, the OAC marathon group mostly used a nine-day schedule during this year’s 12-week buildup to both Boston and New York. No two weeks start or finish the same, but it’s a cycle with room for three long or hard sessions with two or three days of easier running in between—especially important while training at 5,400 feet, Thweatt says.

“The nine-day schedule just made sense because at altitude, with as hard as they’re running our harder sessions, we just need to make sure that we’re absorbing that training—not losing the recovery piece of it,” she explains.

At the peak of the New York build, the OAC runners logged 118 to 135 miles per week, depending on each runner’s preference and background. Klecker started his training early in July to boost his volume and eventually pushed his max to more than 130 miles a few times this fall. Ford and Obiri found their sweet spot around 120, and Kiprop, who previously averaged 100, settled in at about 110.

The biggest pieces of that volume were 35K (22-mile) and 40K (25-mile) long runs, including a couple of them at 8,500 feet on Magnolia Road west of Boulder. On the four 40K runs late in the block, Klecker, Ford, and Kiprop started at about 5:45 mile pace and worked down to 5:30 through 20K, then progressed to 5:20 for most of the final 20K, often closing near 5:00 pace.

Thweatt calls those long runs the bread and butter of the OAC training, but the key is balancing that volume and the harder, faster workouts with slower running on easy days.

After those key long runs, the OAC athletes typically run about six miles “super easy,” Thweatt says, which for them usually means as slow as 7:15 pace but as fast as 6:45 pace. Thweatt has been trying to make sure the athletes (especially Klecker and Obiri) run at those paces on their easy days to ensure they’re optimizing recovery.

The next day, the runners log double sessions of 10 miles in the morning and five miles in the afternoon, followed the next day by 12 miles in the morning and six miles in the afternoon. Those low-key maintenance runs give the mind and body a break, setting them up for one of their signature spicier workouts.

“So between big long runs or bigger sessions, we usually give them three easy days,” Thweatt says. “So you’re not touching those faster paces for three days, but you’re still getting that good quality time on feet and making sure the body is absorbing that last hard session before we hit it again with another one. Recovery is so important and it’s a piece not everyone likes to talk about as much because it's not as flashy as the big workout days.”

Two other staples of the team’s NYC build-up included 10- to 12-mile tempo runs and long, hard fartleks. The tempo runs usually start at 5:00 pace and get faster (Kiprop recently closed one at 4:45 pace), while a sample fartlek alternates “1K on” (2:50-2:55, or 4:35-4:40 mile pace) and “1K off” (3:10, or 5:05 mile pace).

“It’s about being uncomfortable for long periods of time and still trying to shift gears at the end to remind them what it’s going to be like in the marathon,” Thweatt says. “We’re trying to mirror the surges of a marathon in our workouts.”

In the final weeks, the runners also did several VO2 max sessions on the track, including two sets of 1600, 1200, 800, and 400 meters at about 5K pace, which for the OAC’s men comes out to 4:20, 3:12, 2:06, and 1:02, with the second set slightly quicker.

That kind of work has been a big change for Ford, but it has paid off.

“I was somebody that would try to approach marathon training by running at marathon pace and get really comfortable with that. But I think that only works to a certain extent,” says Ford, who just turned 29. “When I was running 2:08 to 2:09, I’d kind of be off of the pack running my own race. Now I am able to stay with the front pack and compete better.”

Unlike Chicago, Berlin, London, or Valencia, which involve mostly flat courses you can run at an even pace, the New York City Marathon is on a rolling course and pace surges play a big role in how the race plays out, Thweatt says.

Ritzenhein and Thweatt believe runners aiming for success in New York have to be able to tap into quicker-cadence running on a moment’s notice to match the terrain and competitive pickups. For example, while runners will do much of the first 16 miles at an even pace, it’s not uncommon for the lead packs to get split apart by frontrunners ratcheting up the pace (often sub-4:25 for men and sub-5:15 for women) on the 3.5-mile rolling, slightly uphill section along First Avenue on the way to the Bronx.

“Those fast track sessions in the middle to the end of a build allow us to spike the system so you can have that speed in the well for the moments you need to shift gears in a race,” Thweatt says. “With the marathon, especially with where the event is at right now with the depth and fast times, you have to touch that speed in training if you want to be competitive in the race. You can increase your volume and do longer workout sessions, but you can’t just do everything at threshold or marathon pace. It’s really important to keep that system firing and to keep it sharp so you have that speed when you need it.”

Ford credits the faster workouts for lowering his half marathon PR by 71 seconds in January (59:48) and his marathon PR by more than two minutes in Boston. He recently ran a 25K version of the 1K on/1K off fartlek, clocking a 1:03 half marathon in the middle of it.

“The reality is you’ll spend time running slower than marathon pace and you’ll spend time running faster [in New York],” he says. “Now that I’ve kind of reached this new level with the faster training with these guys, the approach is more like, ‘Let’s go to New York and try to compete with that front group.’”

Brian Metzler is a Boulder, Colorado, writer and editor whose work has appeared in Runner’s World, Sports Illustrated, ESPN, Outside, Trail Runner, The Chicago Tribune, and Red Bulletin. He’s a former walk-on college middle-distance runner who has transitioned to trail running and pack burro racing in Colorado.

#8908. Menopause and mental health: The science of the menopausal brain

Reviewed by Brian St. Pierre, MS, RD and Helen Kollias, PhD

On a Friday night, as my husband and I tried to figure out where to eat, a typical conversation would go like this:

Me: Do you want to go to that restaurant?

Me: I can’t think of the name. We’ve eaten there before. It’s that place with the peanut shells on the floor? It’s next to… You know… It’s on that road where we used to take the dog to the vet. Do you know the one I’m talking about??

It was as if certain details got lost in a pile of sludge in the deep recesses of my brain. Then, hours later, the details would escape, and I’d shout into an empty room…

However, what seemed to be happening to me, increasingly in my late 40s and early 50s, felt far from typical.

Not only could I never seem to spit out the names of various restaurants or people or books or movies or so many other things, but my brain was also pooping out during the workday.

I’d sit in front of my computer screen, stare at a document, and will myself to do something constructive with my fingertips. Everything seemed hazy, like those first few moments in the morning when you’re awake enough to turn off the alarm but too sleepy to do basic math.

I had my good moments, usually in the morning, when I attempted to pack eight hours of writing into the two or three hours I possessed mental clarity.

On my worst days, however, I awoke with a haze I never managed to shake. Work was a non-starter. Nor did I have enough bandwidth to read, or do much of anything, really.

Three healthcare professionals recommended antidepressants. I tried one, and felt even worse. I tried another. I tried yet another at a higher dose. Still, I felt like a zombie. Another professional gave me a sleeping pill. It left me feeling even more drugged.

Someone tested my thyroid. There was nothing wrong with it. Nor was I anemic. I tried supplements, mushroom coffee, and just about any product with the word “think” somewhere on its label.

Finally, after nearly two years of seeing a revolving door of doctors, I made an appointment with a gynecologist for my yearly exam. I mentioned vaginal dryness. That information triggered her to ask a string of questions that had nothing to do with my undercarriage. How was my sleep? Mood? Energy levels? Was I experiencing hot flashes? How about brain fog?

“Funny you should mention brain fog,” I said in my usual hazy monotone. “I feel like I’m barely alive.”

By the end of the visit, I understood that I’d likely never had depression.

My gynecologist sent me home with prescriptions for estradiol and progesterone.

Within days, it was as if someone had flipped a switch.

I could think again. I could type words again. I could follow conversations. I could work past noon.

And, for the first time in years, I could sleep more than two hours without waking.

Our biggest price drop of the year. Learn to help anyone eat better and get lasting results, whether you're starting a coaching career or leveling up the one you have. Ends Friday.

Instead, like puberty, it’s a life stage—a transitional moment to be precise.

Once you’ve gone 12 consecutive months without a period, you’ve reached menopause. And from that moment onwards, you’re officially “postmenopausal.”

As women approach this transitional moment, hormone levels fluctuate and fall, triggering dozens of symptoms. Weight gain and reduced sex drive get a lot of attention.

However, during and after menopause, roughly 40 percent of women report increased irritability, mood swings, anxiety, fatigue, and trouble concentrating, according to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists.1 2 As the following image shows, it’s also one of the most vulnerable times in a woman’s life to develop depression,3 particularly if they’ve struggled in the past with it before.

Before starting hormones, I often found myself sobbing for no reason. Other times, the world’s stimuli felt too… stimulating.

Normal everyday sounds—like the buzz of traffic or people at the mall—literally hurt. I was jumpy and irritable and felt anxious about situations that had never bothered me in the past, such as driving over bridges or through construction.

Fluctuating hormone levels likely play a role, as do typical age-related changes in the brain.

In addition, during this stage of life, women often deal with several issues that siphon cognitive capacity faster than a thirsty vampire drains a carotid.

During their 40s and 50s, for example, many women have reached the peak of their careers, with responsibilities that follow them home and keep them up at night. They may also be parenting angst-filled teens, caring for aging parents, adjusting to an empty nest, questioning their marriage, or trying to wrap their bank account around the latest statement from the college bursar or hospital billing department.

However, one of the lesser-known and talked about triggers for cognitive discontent has nothing to do with aging or life stress and everything to do with that hallmark menopausal symptom: the hot flash.

Hot flashes, which happen during the day, and night sweats, which occur at night, fall under the category of vasomotor symptoms. (The word “vasomotor” refers to the constriction or dilation of blood vessels which, in turn, can influence everything from blood pressure to sweating.)

During a hot flash or night sweat, norepinephrine and cortisol levels rise. Blood vessels dilate in an attempt to shed heat. Blood pressure and heart rate increase.

Depending on the severity of the hot flash, your skin might redden as sensations of warmth spread through your face, neck, and chest.

You might sweat, experience heart palpitations, or feel anxious, tired, or faint.4

It’s not entirely clear why hot flashes crop up around menopause.

According to one theory, falling estrogen levels affect the hypothalamus, the area of the brain involved in temperature regulation. The brain’s internal thermostat gets wonky and occasionally thinks your body is too hot or cold (when it’s not).

For many years, experts thought of vasomotor symptoms as mere inconveniences or sources of embarrassment.

(To be honest, so did I. During all of those fruitless visits to various healthcare professionals, it never occurred to me to mention them.)

However, an increasing body of research has revealed that hot flashes may do more than make us uncomfortable or force us to change our sheets in the middle of the night.

They may also affect our blood vessels and brains—and not for the better.5 For this reason, an increasing number of experts now consider vasomotor symptoms to be a treatable medical condition.6 7 8

In one study, researchers asked 226 women to wear monitors that tracked when they were experiencing a hot flash. The women also underwent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), filled out sleep diaries, and wore smartwatches that recorded how often they woke at night.9

As researchers looked at the brain images obtained from women who experienced the most hot flashes, they noticed an abundance of patchy areas called whole-brain white matter intensities.

These lesions were once thought of as a typical consequence of aging. However, neuroscientists now believe that the presence of whole-brain white matter intensities is predictive of future cognitive decline.

People with an abundance of these brain lesions are twice as likely to get diagnosed with dementia and three times as likely to have a future stroke.10

It’s thought that the increased presence of whole-brain white matter intensities may stem, in part, from changes taking place in the blood vessels that feed the brain.

A three-year study of 492 women supports that theory. It determined that women who experienced frequent hot flashes also tended to experience unhealthy changes in their blood vessels, such as an inability to dilate to accommodate increased blood flow.11

Other research has linked frequent hot flashes with increases in the following:

In addition to directly affecting the blood vessels, frequent hot flashes may also affect the brain by disturbing sleep.17

Interestingly, many women don’t necessarily know that hot flashes are disturbing their sleep.

They may instead—as I did—assume they have insomnia or sleep apnea.

That’s because night sweats aren’t always sweaty.

By the time a surge in cortisol and norepinephrine jolts a woman awake, the hotness of the flash may have dissipated. So, it can feel as if she’s repeatedly waking, over and over and over again, for no discernable reason.

These frequent awakenings may interfere with the brain’s ability to consolidate memories, metabolize toxins, and store all the names, dates, and facts one encounters daily.

It can also lead to lost connectivity in the hippocampus, a part of the brain that’s important for learning and memory.

Sleep loss also means the amygdala, a part of the brain involved in emotion, becomes more reactive, causing people to feel more easily stressed, anxious, irritable, frustrated, or enraged.18 19

All of these brain changes can set in after just days to a week of lost sleep. So, imagine what happens when you’ve been waking over and over again—for years.

To diagnose depression, healthcare professionals use a tool called the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9) depression scale. If you check off four of the nine symptoms on the scale, you’re considered depressed.

However, four of the symptoms on the checklist also overlap with the symptoms of menopause-related sleep deprivation:

Check off those four items, and you might be diagnosed with depression, even if what’s really ailing you is the battle with sleep you’ve been waging since you turned 47.

Another problem: On surveys, 80 percent of medical residents admit they feel “barely comfortable” talking about menopause.20 In addition, few residency programs—including ob-gyn residency programs—offer training in it.21

Given the above, it’s no wonder so many healthcare professionals never think to ask about hot flashes or sleep disturbances when people like me show up complaining of fatigue, lack of gumption, and an inability to focus.

In addition, even when it’s clear that vasomotor symptoms are leading to cognitive and emotional symptoms, many healthcare professionals still shy away from prescribing menopausal hormone therapy (also called hormone replacement therapy, or HRT), often telling women that supplemental hormones are “not safe” or “too risky.”

These professionals are practicing what Michigan-based menopause-trained gynecologist Jerrold H. Weinberg, MD, calls “defensive medicine.”

“It’s one of the first reflexes doctors have when they recommend a treatment,” says Dr. Weinberg. “They worry they’re going to get sued.”

These worries are based on research done several decades ago that linked the use of certain types of hormones with a slightly increased risk of developing breast cancer or stroke.22

However, according to more recent research, that small increased risk seems to depend on several other factors, such as age, dose, the type of hormonal preparation, and the duration of hormone use.23 24

As long as you’re younger than 60 and have been postmenopausal for fewer than 10 years, many experts now say the benefits outweigh the risks for women with moderate to severe menopausal symptoms.25

It’s also counterbalanced by health benefits such as reduced risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease or osteoporosis, says Dr. Weinberg, who confirms the health benefits of menopause hormone therapy far outweigh the risks for most women.

Because some antidepressants can lift mood, improve sleep, and reduce hot flashes, some healthcare professionals turn to them instead of menopause hormone therapy. As with any medicine, antidepressants have their own list of side effects. However, for someone practicing defensive medicine, they often seem like a safer bet, says Dr. Weinberg.26 27 28

If you or your client are on what seems like a never-ending quest to find a healthcare professional who understands menopause, use the following advice from Dr. Weinberg and Helen Kollias, PhD, an expert on physiology and molecular biology and science advisor at Precision Nutrition and Girls Gone Strong.

▶ Seek care from a menopause-trained health professional.

Usually, these professionals list this training and interest in their bio. For example, they might list “menopause” as an area of focus.

You can also search this database for practitioners who have earned a certification from the Menopause Society.

Write them down. That way, if you feel foggy or nervous during your appointment, you can lean on your notes.

This information can also help you judge whether MHT or another medicine is working. Based on your symptom data, you and your healthcare professional may decide to switch to a different medicine or change your dose.

▶ Be as specific as you can during your appointment.

Saying something like “I don’t sleep well,” is less likely to get you the right kind of help than saying, “During the past seven days, I’ve only gotten four uninterrupted hours once. I wake, on average, five times a night. On a typical night, my longest stretch of sleep is three hours.”

If you use a smartwatch, come ready to fire up your health app, so your healthcare professional can see the data.

▶ Talk about the pros and cons of treatment.

There’s a concept in medicine known as “shared decision-making.” Part of that process involves frank discussions about the benefits and risks of a given treatment. Then, patients and clinicians work together to make decisions based on those benefits and risks.

Many healthcare networks encourage clinicians to use shared decision-making, as it seems to reduce patient complaints as well as malpractice lawsuits.29 30

For this reason, shared decision-making can help shift a healthcare professional out of the “defensive medicine” mindset.

The lifestyle habits that improve mental and emotional health during menopause aren’t terribly different from the lifestyle habits that improve overall health—for any person, at any stage of life.

Other than avoiding caffeine, alcohol, and spicy or hot foods, there’s no special diet for people with vasomotor symptoms. (And by the way, tofu and other soy products don’t seem to help with vasomotor symptoms as much as once thought30—though they’re still nutritious.)

Healthy behaviors don’t necessarily change during middle age.

Nutrition, physical activity, stress management, sleep, social connectedness, and a sense of purpose matter just as much during the menopausal transition as they do when we’re younger. However, these fundamentals are even more important to dial in as life progresses.

If you answered “no” to some or all of those questions, consider why that is. What’s stopping you? How might you remove barriers or shore up support to make those fundamentals easier?

In addition to helping to blunt age- and hormone-related losses in muscle and bone mass, creatine may also help bolster mood and brain function while reducing mental fatigue.

It also seems to counter some of the negative effects of sleep deprivation. 32 33 Research shows a daily dose of 5 to 7 grams of creatine monohydrate is effective.

In addition to helping you feel alert, sunlight helps to set the internal clock in your brain that makes you sleepy at night and spunky in the morning. Morning and late afternoon light exposure seem particularly potent.

In a study of 103 people, exposure to morning sunlight predicted better sleep quality the following night. When people spent time outdoors in the mornings, they fell asleep more quickly, slept longer, and experienced fewer awakenings the following evening.34

Sunlight may also improve mood and concentration.35

If you’re already worn out, long, intense exercise sessions will likely make you feel worse.

For one, injuries crop up much more easily at middle age than during our 20s and 30s. In addition, it takes longer to recover between sessions.36

String too many overly zealous workouts too close together, and you’ll not only likely start to feel achy but also more irritable, tense, and tired.

However, much like a cold shower, short bursts of exercise may help you to feel alert during the day.

If you’re falling asleep at your desk, encourage yourself to take short movement breaks such as a 5- or 10-minute walk outdoors or a quick set of pushups or squats.

In addition, you may find gentle exercise—such as yoga or stretching—helps you relax before bed. Just don’t make it too intense, or you’ll trigger a release of adrenaline.

Whenever you exercise, tune into how your body feels, especially after a particularly bad night of sleep.

We’re not saying you should never exercise vigorously or try to beat your lifting PRs. However, depending on your sleep and recovery, you might want to pare things back, especially if you’ve traditionally hit the gym hard.

You can still do intense sessions—just balance them out with more moderate sessions, as well as proportionate recovery.

Depending on how you feel, you might decide to go all out, as usual.

However, you might also decide to do a zone 2 training session instead of an intense run. Or, if you’re resistance training, you might still do your planned session, but reduce the number of sets, reps, or volume lifted.

This research-based therapy for insomnia can help you develop skills and mental reframes that encourage sound sleep.

For example, a CBT-I therapist will help you develop the skill of getting up at the same time every day, regardless of how badly you slept (or didn’t sleep) the night before.

(Read more: Three CBT-I skills that can transform how you sleep.)

You may not have the energy (or desire) to do everything you did when you were younger. (When you were 36, your daily checklist defied time and space.)

As a result, you might benefit from looking critically at your current responsibilities to see which ones you can shrink or downsize. For several days, track how you spend your time and bandwidth. Then, analyze your data.

If you’re a coach, use the Wheel of Stress Assessment to help clients identify different dimensions of their life that might be draining their mental and emotional capacity. (When you know specifically where your stress is coming from, you have a better chance of resolving it.)

If it’s demands from other people that prevent you from prioritizing self-care and recovery, you might like to read: How saying “no” can seriously change your life.

You might find you sleep better and experience fewer night sweats if you sleep in a cooler environment.

Try turning down the thermostat a couple of degrees, using a fan, or investing in an electric cooling mattress pad.

When you feel the fog take over your brain, it’s not likely you’ll be doing “your best work” anyway.

So, for a block of time—say, 20 minutes—permit yourself to do nothing. You might:

If you need a quick “refresh,” you can also try a 5-minute mind-body scan.

Get your body into a comfortable position. For example, you might use the yoga “legs up the wall” pose or lie down and place a pillow under your knees.

Then, close your eyes and bring your attention to physical sensations in your body. Start at your head, and work your way down to your toes.

Don’t judge or rush to change anything. Just observe, like a scientist. You can also scan your mind, for example, by noticing thoughts.

When you’ve completed the scan, consider:

You don’t have to “do” anything with the information you uncover, just notice.

The foods that protect the blood vessels around your heart can also protect the blood vessels in your brain.

For example, both the MIND and Mediterranean diets are associated with a reduced risk of Alzheimer’s disease and depression.37 38 These eating patterns are rich in vegetables, fruit, whole grains, olives, beans, fish, and other minimally-processed whole foods.

In addition, nitrate-rich foods like beets and dark, leafy greens may help to dilate blood vessels, temporarily improving memory by helping more blood to reach the brain.39 40

(For more on how our diet can support brain function and emotional regulation, read: Nutrition and mental health: What (and how) to eat)

It’s frustrating when you feel like you can’t do it all.

However, this stage of life presents a hidden opportunity, forcing you to re-evaluate what’s most important.

Before going on hormones, as my ability to type coherent words and phrases diminished, I was forced to ask an important question:

It was more of an existential question than a career-related one, and it allowed me to reassess how I wanted to spend my limited mental resources.

Given that I was self-employed, I didn’t actually need to be working eight hours a day. That was a gift, wasn’t it?

Maybe I also didn’t need to cook dinner six nights out of seven. Maybe the recipes I chose could be simplified, too.

Finally, maybe saying “no” a lot more often and without regret would allow me to continue to say yes to the things that mattered most.

And picking up the phone whenever my kid called from college.

Or meeting a friend for a meandering walk around town.

Thanks to the hormones and life tweaks, I now have energy again. I’m also clear-headed most of the time. However, I still tend to end my work day around 3 p.m.

#8907. I’ve Run 14 Marathons. Here Are My 5 Race Recovery Tips to Get You Running Again Soon.

How to ease soreness, refuel well, and rebuild motivation after crossing 26.2.

Ask any marathoner: There is nothing like the energy of race weekend to get you amped up to keep on running. Feeling the weight of that finisher’s medal hanging around your neck has a magical way of erasing all the aches and exhaustion you pushed through for the past few hours (not to mention the past several months of training).

But what you do in the hours and days immediately following 26.2 miles can determine how quickly you bounce back—not only physically but also how soon you’ll feel emotionally ready to get moving again. Marathons are draining, and that finish-line euphoria won’t keep sustaining you through continuous daily runs if you don’t let yourself recover fully.

After conquering 14 marathon finish lines in all seasons and a few back-to-back marathons too, I’ve learned a few key lessons about how to successfully get back to running postrace. Keep these in mind if you’ve just crossed a marathon off your list and want to lace up your running shoes again soon.

The first time I ran the New York City Marathon, I lived in a fifth-floor walk-up apartment on the Upper East Side. Going down those stairs the next day was excruciating, but I went outside anyway and went for a walk—and my legs felt immensely better a day later, compared with when I didn’t take those steps after other races.

Obviously, you should give yourself some downtime and relax after a marathon, but when I make a point to walk around more often right after a race and to do some other light activity (like easy pedaling on my Peloton) over the following few days, it always helps my legs feel way better sooner. Sitting on the couch all day will only increase your stiffness.

Regardless of whether you hit a PR, qualified for Boston, or barely made it over the finish line, completing a marathon is a big accomplishment. I’ve found that taking some time after 26.2 to celebrate and appreciate my body for what it can do—and my mind for what it can push through—is an important step before jumping right back into running. When I push ahead without taking joy and pride in what I achieved, I wind up feeling run down and unmotivated.

If you feel like having a decadent meal and celebratory beers as part of that acknowledgment, Jeff Gaudette, owner and head coach at RunnersConnect, says go for it! But to feel up to running again soon, have something nutritious first.

“The focus on recovery needs to be more dialed in if you're going to do another race soon,” he says. “That means nutrition and refueling a little more diligently. You can still enjoy pizza and beer, but make sure you get some protein and healthy carbs beforehand.”

Research backs this nutrient combo up: One 2018 study in Nutrients found that eating both carbs and protein immediately postrace helped marathoners’ physical fatigue, mental energy, and soreness improve within three days compared with those who ate carbs alone.

Your body just did a lot; give it some extra TLC to help your muscles recover faster. Gaudette recommends trying out all the “little recovery tricks”—ice baths, dips in a hot tub, a massage—and seeing what helps you get back to 100 percent faster.

My fave: slipping on compression socks after a marathon and sleeping in them, too. Wearing them feels like my calves are getting a hug, and I always think my legs are a little less sore the next day when I use them. (Some research also backs up the benefits of compression gear for easing postexercise soreness.)

If you already have another race approaching, recovery is even more important—as is the training you put in between races. My worst marathon performances were when I ran Boston to Big Sur (both races within two weeks); I had not trained well enough for the hills and probably didn’t do enough to help my body recover between the races, and I paid for it.

How you structure recovery and training between two races depends on how much time you have. “If they’re really close, like within two weeks, the entire focus is on recovery and getting your legs to feel as good as possible,” says Gaudette. (See: ice baths, massage, etc.) “If there’s a longer break between, say three to six weeks, then after you fully recover, you'll want to have a week or two where you do some mileage and/or solid threshold work. Otherwise, you risk basically not training for five to six weeks—including the taper before the first race and then the time between the races.”

That’s enough time for your fitness to fall off and you to feel less prepared for race number two.

If you don’t already have a race on the calendar, use that finish-line motivation you’re feeling now to look ahead for another race you want to take on, even if it’s months away.

I never feel as energized to take on another marathon as right after I finish one (and the days leading up to it). I’ve learned I’m most likely to sign up for another race if I use that momentum to register for one. And with your next race on the books—whether you’ll be aiming for a PR in another marathon or going for a chill 5K with friends—it’s that much easier to get back to running and clock miles consistently because the goal is right in front of you.
