#8857. What Happens When Grief Derails Your Triathlon Training

Rachel Olson wins 2026 Ironman 70.3 São Paulo after struggling to train through the grief of losing her mother in November 2024. (Photo: Romulo Cruz/Ironman)

In late September, Rachel Olson crossed the finish line first at Ironman 70.3 São Paulo, nearly 10 minutes ahead of her nearest competitor. The race, by her own admission, was “not spectacular” for the longtime pro triathlete. But the support that followed was. The crowd embraced her, and athletes and fans who had followed her story cheered a little louder, as though they knew what it took just to get her to the start line.

Because in the months after her mother Janis died in November 2024 of liver disease, Olson could barely bring herself to work out. She did not want to disappear from triathlon. But she’d go to the pool and just sit on the edge and cry. She’d hop on her bike and feel a sudden urge to turn around. Running, always an easy way to manage big emotions, became a chore.

Then her body began to rebel: digestive issues, mysterious inflammation, bone-deep exhaustion, muscles that wouldn’t recover.

“My body was basically screaming at me that something was wrong, like it was constantly fighting something,” said Olson, 35, who lives in Boulder with her fiancé, fellow pro triathlete Andre Lopes. “Your mind is telling you to process, and your body is telling you to slow down.”

For endurance athletes, the instinct after a loss is often to train through the emotional pain. The adage goes that exercise helps with grief: Get outside, move your body, clear your head. Sometimes it does. But for Olson and many others, the very thing that once gave life structure can become one more demand on a body and mind already stretched thin.

“Grief doesn’t just live in the mind. It’s in the chest, in the restlessness, in this low-grade energy that has nowhere obvious to go,” said Kenza Haddock, president and co-founder of Oceanic Counseling Group in Murrells Inlet, South Carolina. “Endurance sport can tip from processing grief into outrunning it, using exhaustion to stay ahead of the feeling rather than move through it. It can just leave you more numb.”

Plenty of endurance athletes have turned grief into a mission. In August 2026, Matthew Hollingham, a 25-year-old doctoral student at Penn State, created an “Arctic Circle to Africa” triathlon in memory of his late fiancée Lovisa Arnesson-Cronhamre, who was killed in a hit-and-run while jogging on campus. Over 61 days and 3,545 miles, he swam in a lake above the Arctic Circle, ran a marathon a day for 37 days, and cycled just over 110 miles a day for 23. He raised more than $40,000 for two charities and kept her memory present.

Others have taken similar routes; at the 2026 London Marathon, Laura Coleman-Day, a 33-year-old mother from Lincolnshire in the U.K., went viral for changing into her wedding dress and running the final miles in it as a dedication to her late husband, Xander.

This kind of public mission can be cathartic, says Hilary Bucell, a psychotherapist and lecturer at Columbia University.

“Engaging in something like triathlon can become a ritualized space where the recognition of the loss is welcomed and at the same time, the sport’s necessity for present moment awareness also helps athletes acknowledge new life experiences continuing now beyond the loss,” she said.

Of course, racing to honor a loved one doesn’t erase grief — it just gives you a place to put it. It can also offer a healthy distraction from the deep ache of a devastating loss.

Some aren’t able to navigate their grief in such a public and profound way. There are those like Olson whose grief hits the body hard enough to derail training. In 2023, Gustav Iden, the 2022 Ironman World Champion, ended his season early to heal and regroup after the death of his mother, revealing “it was very emotional, and it was hard to find joy in training after that.” (He returned to racing about a year later.)

As one of her mother’s main caretakers, Olson spent two years before her death flying to her hometown in Texas for doctor’s appointments. Triathlon took a backseat: She parted ways with her coach and scaled back her training. Even when she did have time to work out, anxiety followed.

“I would think, ‘Am I going to be out on a bike ride and get a phone call saying she’s in the hospital? Are things going to go downhill?’”

After Janis died, that anxiety turned physical. Olson was never diagnosed with one specific issue, but testing showed elevated inflammation markers and low ferritin, requiring an iron infusion.

“Ultimately, I think my body was responding to trauma. It felt like I had an illness,” she said. “Trying to perform in a body that felt completely foreign to me was incredibly difficult. I didn’t understand why my body wasn’t doing what it had done before.”

Research suggests that grief can affect the body as well as the mind. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) lists impaired immune response and increased mortality from heart disease, especially in older, widowed patients, among the physical complications. The effects may vary, as not everyone experiences the same physical response.

Part of the explanation may lie in how the brain processes the loss of a loved one through interconnected systems involved in emotion, threat detection, and the regulation of stress hormones. Grief can flood the body with inflammatory signals. and increase cortisol, the steroid hormone produced by the adrenal glands that regulates the body’s response to stress.

“Grief is a neurological event that impacts your ability to learn and remember things, attend to things, and impacts your mood,” said Wilfred van Gorp, a Manhattan-based board-certified neuropsychologist. “Losing someone keeps your amygdala on high alert and elevates cortisol. It impacts you in your body as well as your mind.”

Grief and stress can also disrupt communication between the brain and the gut, which may contribute to everything from irritable bowel syndrome to acid reflux to ulcers, according to research.

For Olson, whose stomach swelled within days of her mother’s death, that brain-gut link was obvious.

“Only two days after [she passed], I woke up, and my stomach was distended about five inches. And then I kind of exploded in inflammation weight,” she shared. “Trying to get that down is not an easy process.”

Still, Olson pushed on. She’d qualified for her first Ironman World Championship slated for about 10 months after Janis died. She wanted to race there to honor her mom. She also didn’t want to lose her identity as a triathlete. Her training “wasn’t even close” to peak levels. In Kona, her stomach rebelled on the bike. After vomiting for three hours, she pulled out soon after starting the run.

“I held onto triathlon so tightly even though my body wasn’t ready. My mind wasn’t ready,” Olson said. “I kept pushing because I wanted it so badly. I attached too much weight to needing training [and racing] to go well and needing something in my life to be OK. Looking back, I realize I didn’t have to be OK.”

After Kona, Olson took a break. She focused on her other jobs as a triathlon coach and as a sales rep, and on envisioning what her wedding to Lopes could look like without her mom.

“I decided I wasn’t going to think about triathlon for a couple of weeks,” she shared. “If I still wanted it afterward, great. If I didn’t, that was OK, too.”

Spoiler: She still loved it. With the fog lifted, Olson saw a different future in the sport, starting with a new coach, Kasper Pedersen, who could build a sustainable load and understand her fragile state.

“I looked for a coach who understands that life happens,” said Olson. “Kasper is great at helping me push my boundaries, but he also knows that I may need to go at my own pace.”

They’re keeping her training volume relatively low as she re-establishes a baseline and repairs her frayed central nervous system.

“I really wanted to make my body and mind think, ‘This is fun. This is helping us,’ rather than setting off alarm bells every time I went out,” Olson shared. “There are still days where I have to take some time off. … Grief really is a roller coaster. But overall, we’ve done a really good job of figuring out what is working.”

Talking about it helps, too, though it doesn’t come easily. Olson describes her grief as a “cloud over her personal life,” and opening up about it has cost her: One friend drifted away, unable to understand what she was going through. Olson wonders if she was simply too much to handle. Still, she finds solace in speaking out, and in being a voice for others who may be grieving alone.

“As athletes, we want to put difficult things in the back of our minds and keep going,” she said. “But I’m glad I can be a voice for other people who are going through the same so they feel less alone than they think they are.”

If her recent win in Brazil is any sign, Olson is rounding a bend toward healing, with an approach to triathlon (and life) that’s less about control and more about leaning into the process, however unpredictable and messy it may be.

“I feel like I’m a different person than I was before [my mom died]. It will always feel like a part of me has been ripped away. But I also know that there’s literally no pain that hurts as bad as what I went through,” she said. “So I’ll keep telling myself, ‘Yes, I can do this thing.’”

#8856. ZOLTÁN BÁTHORY OF FIVE FINGER DEATH PUNCH IS COMMITTED TO HIS MUSIC, COMMUNITIES, AND JUDO

The members of Five Finger Death Punch have been busy lately. Their 10th studio album, Legacy, was recently released, and they began their 20th Anniversary World Tour in July with the North American leg. Zoltán Báthory is the founder of 5FDP as well as their rhythm guitarist and primary songwriter. When asked his thoughts about celebrating two decades of success, Báthory was proud but more grateful for their legions of fans.

“It was always the people’s band,” he said with a smile. The Las Vegas band has been around so long, they were first getting attention on MySpace. Báthory recalled experts writing in magazines that they wouldn’t be around very long, but staying true to themselves and focusing only on the music has been their key to success.

“We just kept pushing and the people stayed with us.”

Báthory knows their music is not for everybody, but he hears stories all the time from people who have told them that hits such as “Under and Over It” and “Wash it All Away” are on their workout playlists or may have helped them get past a hard time in their lives. Báthory views that as a badge of honor because he himself trains in Flex Lewis’ Dragon Lair gym in Las Vegas and is as much a part of that community as he is the hard rock and heavy metal space.

“I’m proud of that because these are my people.”

5FDP also has a large following in the military and first responder communities. Aside from their many hits, they are known for their support of veterans and firefighters through donations to the Call of Duty Endowment fund, doing other fundraisers through their music, and Báthory has served on boards for groups like the Home Deployment Project.

“When I get a military guy telling me, ‘It’s difficult to be in a war zone. But I got up every day and listened to you guys, and it not just got me ready for the day, it got me through the day.’ That kind of gives us a justification that we’re doing something good. So, it also keeps us going. I love it.”

Báthory’s love for music and working out may only be rivaled by his passion for judo. Growing up in Hungary, judo in his home country was more popular than it is in North America. He first started following the discipline at age 9 and was entering tournaments before becoming a teenager. Báthory felt that taking up judo has done far more for him than improving his skills alone.

“I can say and I can claim that that philosophy of judo was one of the key elements of me becoming successful,” he explained. “It rewires your mind, and you start to think very differently.”

Báthory still makes time to train and actively competes in tournaments to this day. He has also taken up jiujitsu and reports having black belts in both disciplines. But he is not only trying to be better in martial arts but for it as well. Judo is an Olympic sport, and athletes internationally are very committed to excelling in it. The American judo scene is not as prominent as it is in other countries, but Báthory is trying to change that and wants to help those Americans looking to compete in the 2028 Summer Olympic Games in Los Angeles, California.

“I’ve worked with USA Judo and IJF (International Judo Federation). It’s one of my missions to make judo more visible in America, for more people to practice it.”

Báthory’s passion and commitment to his mission is more than moral support and advocacy. He has even made a financial commitment to this goal.

“I want the American team to do really well in judo. I’m even financially supporting the judo team. A portion of the tickets of this tour is actually going to USA Judo so they can afford the participation in training camps.”

Even though they have two decades behind them, 5FDP is as popular as ever, and tickets to their shows have already been selling fast. Like any elite band, they have had their shares of growing pains and critics, but the loyal fanbase and joy they get from creating music and performing it continues to fuel their desire.

Báthory has as much love and appreciation for their supporters as they do for the band. That’s because of the communities those fans are in; military, first responders, athletes, martial arts, and others who are looking for something positive to lean on. Báthory proclaimed that 5FDP will continue to make music and do their best to support their fans not only because they support them but because of what they do.

“What is the common denominator between these people? They all help other people.”

You can learn more about 5FDP, their tour, and Legacy by going to their website and subscribing to their YouTube channel.

Follow Báthory on Instagram @zoltanbathory and @zoltanbjj.

Picture this: you're settled into your seat on a United flight out of LAX, the Pacific stretching endlessly outside your window, and you know — you genuinely know — that the person next to you paid $400 for this exact seat while you paid **7,500 miles**. That's the Hawaiian sweet spot, and it's one of the most quietly powerful redemptions available to anyone building a travel rewards strategy. Hawaii has always been the aspirational American vacation. It's the honeymoon destination, the bucket-list family trip, the anniversary getaway. And because of that demand, flights from the mainland — especially during spring break, summer, and the holidays — rarely go on sale. A round-trip economy ticket from Los Angeles to Honolulu will routinely run **$400–$700**, and during peak travel windows, prices can push past $1,000 for a family of four. That's real money. FI-community money. Now consider what Turkish Airlines Miles & Smiles charges for that same seat: **7,500 miles one-way**. At the low end of cash pricing ($200 for a one-way), you're extracting **2.7 cents per point**. At the high end ($500 during peak season), that same 7,500 miles is worth **6.7 cents per point** — a figure that makes even seasoned travel rewards enthusiasts do a double-take. For context, most people in the points world consider 1.5–2 cents per point a solid redemption. **Getting 6.7 cents per point is extraordinary.** It's not a fluke or a loophole — it's a structural pricing inefficiency baked into the Turkish award chart, which treats all short-haul domestic U.S. flights (including Hawaii, which is technically a domestic route) at the same rock-bottom rate. This is the fundamental insight behind every great travel rewards redemption: **loyalty programs price awards based on their own logic, not cash fares.** Turkish Miles & Smiles sees LAX→HNL as a short Star Alliance partner flight. The fact that cash fares on that route are elevated because of destination demand is irrelevant to their award chart. That gap — between what Turkish charges in miles and what the market charges in dollars — is exactly where you save. For a ChooseFI community member who already holds Citi ThankYou Points, this redemption is within reach right now. You don't need to fly Turkish. You don't need to connect through Istanbul. You just need availability on United, 7,500 miles, and about 20 minutes.

The magic here comes down to one core concept: Star Alliance partner pricing on a domestic U.S. route.

Turkish Airlines is a Star Alliance member, and like most alliance programs, they allow their members to book award flights on partner airlines — including United. Where Turkish gets interesting (and generous) is in how they price those partner awards. Their award chart uses a fixed, distance-based or zone-based structure, and for short-haul U.S. domestic flights, the price bottoms out at 7,500 miles one-way in economy.

Here's the pricing inefficiency in plain language: Turkish Miles & Smiles doesn't care that Hawaii is an aspirational, high-demand destination. To their award chart, LAX→HNL is just another short domestic United flight. Meanwhile, United's own MileagePlus program charges significantly more for the same route — often 13,000–22,500 miles one-way depending on the fare bucket. Turkish is pricing the same seat at less than half what United charges its own members. That's the gap you're exploiting.

No fuel surcharges — ever. This is a critical detail that makes Turkish a standout program. Many European programs (we're looking at you, Lufthansa Miles & More) pile on hundreds of dollars in fuel surcharges that nearly erase the value of the award. Turkish charges zero fuel surcharges on any award flight, including partner redemptions. Your out-of-pocket cost when booking this redemption is taxes and fees only — typically $5–$15 for a domestic U.S. itinerary.

The most accessible path to 7,500 Turkish miles runs through Citi ThankYou Points, which transfer to Turkish at a 1:1 ratio. The transfer is instant — meaning you can see award availability, confirm your plan, and have the miles in your Turkish account within minutes, not days. That speed matters because Hawaii saver availability can disappear quickly.

You can also transfer from Bilt Rewards at 1:1 (also instant), or Marriott Bonvoy at a 3:1 ratio (takes 1–5 days and is far less efficient — avoid Marriott for this transfer unless you have no other option).

The best Citi cards for earning ThankYou Points include the Citi Strata Premier, which earns 3x on dining, groceries, hotels, and airfare — categories that make accumulating 7,500 points genuinely fast for most households.

Turkish's award chart is fixed, meaning the price doesn't fluctuate with demand, time of year, or how close you are to departure (beyond the booking window). A saver economy award on a short domestic U.S. United flight is always 7,500 miles. No dynamic pricing surprises. No "off-peak vs. peak" tiers to navigate. This predictability is itself a feature — you can plan around it.

The booking window opens 355 days in advance, giving you nearly a full year of search runway to find the availability you need.

Here's exactly how to execute this redemption from zero to booked.

Before you transfer a single point, confirm that saver economy availability exists on your target route and dates. Go to united.com, enter your origin and destination (for example, LAX to HNL), and select your travel dates. When the results appear, look specifically for fares labeled "Saver" — these are the award inventory buckets that partner programs like Turkish can access. Standard or Everyday awards will NOT be bookable through Turkish.

Search for "Saver" fares in economy and note the exact flight numbers, dates, and times. Take a screenshot — you'll need these details when you move to the Turkish website.

Tip: United's calendar view lets you scan a full month for saver availability. Use it. Flexibility of even 1–2 days can be the difference between finding a seat and hitting a wall.

Go to turkishairlines.com and navigate to the Miles & Smiles award booking tool. Search the same route and dates you identified on United. Turkish's search engine pulls real-time Star Alliance availability, so what you see here is what you can book. If the saver seats from Step 1 appear, you're ready to move.

Important: If you don't yet have a Turkish Miles & Smiles account, create one now — it's free and takes just a few minutes.

Once you've confirmed award availability, transfer your points. Log into your Citi ThankYou account (or Bilt Rewards account), navigate to the transfer partner section, and select Turkish Airlines Miles & Smiles. Enter the amount — 7,500 points per one-way flight — and confirm.

Citi and Bilt transfers to Turkish are instant. Your miles will appear in your Turkish account within minutes. Do not transfer until you've confirmed availability in Step 2 — points transfers are one-way and non-refundable.

Return to the Turkish award booking tool with your miles now loaded. Complete the booking for your confirmed flight. You'll pay only taxes and fees at checkout — typically $5–$15 for a domestic U.S. itinerary. Enter your payment details for that small amount and complete the reservation.

You'll receive a booking confirmation from Turkish. The actual ticket is on United metal, so you'll also see the reservation appear in United's system using your confirmation code.

Hawaii saver availability on United can be tight, especially during peak travel periods. Here's your playbook:

Let's make this concrete. It's late February, and you're planning a spring getaway to Honolulu with your partner. You pull up United.com and search LAX→HNL for mid-April — not peak spring break week, but the week after, when families have gone home and the island is quieter. You find saver economy availability on a direct United flight departing at 8:45 AM and arriving in Honolulu before noon local time.

The cash price for that ticket: $389 per person one-way. For two travelers, that's $778 before you've booked the return.

The points price: 7,500 Turkish Miles & Smiles miles per person, plus roughly $11 in taxes and fees. For two people, you're spending 15,000 miles and about $22.

You already have 20,000 Citi ThankYou Points sitting in your account from everyday spending on your Citi Strata Premier — groceries, dining, a couple of utility bills. You transfer 15,000 points to Turkish Miles & Smiles (instant transfer), log into the Turkish booking portal, and complete both seats in a single transaction.

Your CPP on this redemption: $389 ÷ 7,500 = 5.2 cents per point. That's more than three times what most people consider a strong redemption.

Now for the experience itself: you're flying United Economy on a widebody aircraft — typically a Boeing 767 or 777 on the Honolulu route from LAX. The flight is approximately 5.5 hours. Economy isn't business class, but United's Pacific routes are comfortable — you'll find decent legroom in Economy Plus if you want to upgrade your seat selection for a modest fee, complimentary entertainment, and meal service on this longer domestic segment. The flight across the Pacific, even in economy, has a different feel than a 2-hour domestic hop. The water below you turns that impossible shade of blue. You land in Honolulu at mid-morning, cleared customs quickly (domestic flight — no customs required), and you're at your hotel before lunch.

Total cost for two one-way tickets: 15,000 miles + $22. Cash equivalent: $778. Money saved: $756. That's a car payment, a month of groceries, or a head start on your next investment contribution — redirected from airline revenue to your FI journey.

The 7,500-mile rate is available year-round — Turkish doesn't have a separate peak pricing tier for this redemption. But United's saver inventory dries up fast during summer, spring break, and the December holidays. Target September through November and January through mid-February for the best combination of availability and lower cash prices (which tells you demand is lower). Mid-week departures (Tuesday, Wednesday) consistently show better saver seat availability than weekend flights.

Turkish's booking window opens 355 days in advance. United releases the bulk of its saver award inventory when the schedule first opens — roughly 11 months before departure. If you have a specific date in mind (say, a milestone anniversary trip), start checking 355 days out and move fast when you see availability.

Book the outbound through Turkish (LAX→HNL, 7,500 miles) and then search for a separate return award. Turkish allows open-jaw itineraries, so you could theoretically fly into Honolulu and return from Maui if routing works. Piece together two one-way awards for maximum flexibility.

This is the single most common mistake. Points transfers to Turkish are irreversible. If you transfer 7,500 points and then discover saver availability has disappeared, those points are in Turkish's system with no easy path back. Always confirm availability on the Turkish booking portal before initiating any transfer.

Marriott Bonvoy transfers to Turkish at a 3:1 ratio and takes 1–5 days. You'd need 22,500 Marriott points to get 7,500 Turkish miles — a terrible rate. Stick with Citi ThankYou or Bilt at 1:1, both instant.

If you're combining this Hawaii redemption with an international Turkish itinerary, Turkish allows free stopovers in Istanbul on connecting itineraries. That's a separate strategy, but worth knowing as your travel portfolio grows.

Turkish miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. Even one small miles transaction — earning or redeeming — resets the clock. Transfer a small batch of points or book a cheap award every few years to keep your account alive.

The math behind one of travel rewards' best-kept secrets

Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles uses a distance-based award chart that treats Hawaii as a domestic U.S. destination. Since flights from the West Coast to Hawaii are under 3,000 miles, they fall into the lowest pricing tier at just 7,500 miles each way. Compare this to United MileagePlus, which charges 22,500 miles each way for the same route through its own program. The Turkish chart effectively gives you a 67% discount for the identical seat on the identical United flight. This pricing anomaly is one of the most valuable in travel rewards and has persisted for years.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Register for a free Miles&Smiles account on the Turkish Airlines website. You will need this account to receive transferred miles and book award flights.

Before transferring miles, verify award space exists. Search on United.com for saver-level award space to Hawaii on your preferred dates. If United shows availability at the saver level, it should be bookable through Turkish.

Transfer Citi ThankYou Points or Capital One Miles to your Turkish Miles&Smiles account at a 1:1 ratio. Allow 24-48 hours for transfers to process. Only transfer once you have confirmed availability.

Log into your Miles&Smiles account and search for your United flight to Hawaii. If the online system does not show the award, call Turkish Airlines customer service to book over the phone. Have your flight details and Miles&Smiles number ready.

After booking, you will receive a Turkish Airlines confirmation. Add your United MileagePlus number to the reservation for elite benefits. You can manage the booking through either Turkish or United once ticketed.

Yes. Turkish Miles&Smiles prices United-operated flights to Hawaii at 7,500 miles each way in economy because its award chart treats Hawaii as a domestic U.S. route. The same seat through United's own program costs 22,500 miles — three times more.

The most practical path is through Citi ThankYou Points, which transfer 1:1 to Turkish Miles&Smiles. The Citi Premier card earns 3x on travel and gas, making it a strong earning tool. Capital One Miles also transfer to Turkish at a 1:1 ratio.

Availability depends on United releasing Star Alliance partner award space (sometimes called "saver" availability). Searching 2-4 months in advance, on weekdays, or during shoulder season (April-May, September-October) significantly improves your chances.

Yes, but the miles cost increases with distance. From the East Coast, flights to Hawaii price at 10,000-12,500 miles each way depending on routing distance. Still an excellent deal compared to United's own pricing, though the West Coast offers the absolute lowest redemption.

This redemption was built for the ChooseFI member who's just starting to take travel rewards seriously — someone who has a Citi credit card, has been accumulating ThankYou Points on everyday spending, and wants their first "I can't believe this worked" moment.

Families planning a Hawaii vacation. At 7,500 miles per person, a family of four needs just 30,000 miles one-way — an achievable balance for anyone who's been strategic with a single Citi card for 6–12 months. The savings versus paying cash for four tickets can easily hit $1,500–$2,000, which is serious FI-community money.

Couples looking for a meaningful but accessible trip. Hawaii is aspirational without requiring long-haul international travel. This is the redemption that converts skeptical partners into believers.

West Coast residents (California, Washington, Oregon, Nevada) who have direct United service to Hawaii from nearby airports. The further you are from direct Hawaii service, the more complex positioning becomes.

Minimum points balance needed: Just 7,500 Citi ThankYou or Bilt points per one-way flight. That's genuinely achievable — even a single welcome bonus on an entry-level Citi card exceeds this threshold.

This redemption is less ideal for travelers on the East Coast (positioning flights eat into the simplicity), anyone without access to Citi or Bilt points (other transfer paths are inefficient), and travelers who need guaranteed availability on specific peak dates — the saver inventory just isn't reliable enough for inflexible itineraries.

This redemption is rated **Easy** in category but carries a few specific friction points worth understanding before you start. The **earning side is straightforward** — 7,500 Citi ThankYou Points is a modest target that most people hit within a few months of regular spending on a Citi Strata Premier. The transfer to Turkish is instant and simple. The **main challenge is availability**. United's saver economy inventory to Hawaii is genuinely limited, especially during popular travel windows. You may search your ideal dates and find nothing. This isn't a bug — it's just the nature of partner award bookings. The program prices this incredibly cheaply *because* the airlines release limited seats at this level. The **booking interface** adds minor friction. The Turkish Miles & Smiles website works, but it's not as polished as booking directly on United.com. Expect a slightly clunky experience — search patiently, and don't be surprised if you need to refresh or try slightly different date combinations. **Three tips to overcome the main challenges:** 1. **Be flexible with dates.** Saver availability is the limiting factor. If you can move your trip by 2–3 days, your chances of finding a seat increase dramatically. 2. **Search early.** Start 10–11 months out. The availability you can't find at 3 months may have been wide open at 11 months. 3. **Confirm before you transfer.** Check the Turkish booking tool *first*, then move your points. This keeps the process clean and stress-free. If you're willing to be slightly flexible on dates, this redemption is genuinely beginner-accessible — and the payoff, especially for a family, makes the modest extra effort completely worthwhile.

The Turkish Miles&Smiles sweet spot for Hawaii flights is one of the most dramatic value plays in travel rewards. Booking the exact same United flight for 7,500 miles instead of 22,500 United miles is a 67% savings, and at cash values of $400-$800+, you are getting 3-5 cents per mile in value. While the booking process can require a phone call and some patience, the savings are substantial enough to make this one of the first sweet spots every travel rewards enthusiast should learn. If you hold Citi ThankYou or Capital One points and want to visit Hawaii, this is your move.

#8853. I Made One Small Change to My Form and Instantly Became a Stronger Runner. You Will, Too.

As soon as I heard this advice, everything clicked.

Even though I’ve been running for a decade, I still often wonder about—okay, occasionally obsess over—my running form.

Is my foot striking the ground properly? Am I moving my arms too much or not enough? Am I using the strength in my legs in a way that maximizes my stride?

It wasn’t until I started watching How to Start Running—Runner’s World’s video program that helps new runners begin a consistent routine with guidance from top experts—that the answer really began to crystallize for me. In one of the program’s chapters, our host, certified personal trainer and run coach Matt Meyer, delivers a simple, but brilliant piece of advice for fine-tuning your running form:

“Drive your knees up,” Meyer says, “and think about pulling your heels up behind you.”

When I’m running, I usually focus on lifting my knees, but I almost never worry about what’s happening behind me. After watching this clip, though, I went on a run and followed Matt’s advice. I made sure that with each step I took, I pulled my heels up toward my glutes. I immediately felt stronger, like I was able to push off more forcefully, propel myself further forward, and make each stride longer.

For the first time in my running life, my form finally feels solid, which has made me a more confident runner. I also learned that even after a decade, it’s okay to go back to the basics.

Yes, How to Start Running changed the way I run. So whether you’re new to running, coming back from an injury, or in need of a form fix like me, give it a try. Matt and other running experts will show you how to start slowly using run/walk intervals that allow you to build upon your progress week after week, plus offer tips to ensure you avoid common beginner missteps that can result in boredom, fatigue, or injury.

For better brain cognition through to superior strength and power, creatine is one of those supplements that seems to actually work. Thanks to its cell volumizing and energizing abilities, creatine allows us to lift heavier, recover faster, and focus better under stress. Now, a new study from Texas A&M University is touting that creatine can construct more muscle even without a structured resistance training program.

The study, published in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, suggests that creatine could help adults to maintain lean tissue and strength, even without regular exercise. Of course, maintaining adequate levels of muscle mass is particularly important as we age because muscle loss, also known as sarcopenia, can begin as early as 35 years, and typically sees lean mass decline at a rate of 1 to 2 percent, per year, for the average person. In fact, those who fail to engage with regular resistance training could lose as much as 4 to 6 pounds of muscle per decade.

New meta-analyses show this tried and true supp can benefit both men and women—but you still have to...

For 12 weeks, men and women between the ages of 45 and 65 were provided with creatine or a maltodextrin placebo, with each group being split into those who wanted to participate in a supervised, structured exercise program, and those who didn’t want to commit to the organized sessions. As the participants filled out questionnaires during the study, data showed that the structured exercise group racked up more moderate-to-vigorous activity than those who weren’t locked in.

Despite lower levels of activity, those who took two 5g doses of creatine per day, and were not in the structured exercise program, increased their lean tissue by around 2.4 pounds over the 12-week study period. Conversely, those who took the placebo lost almost half a pound. “Creatine Monohydrate supplementation without exercise training and diet intervention increased lean tissue mass, strength, and muscular endurance while promoting favorable changes in selected blood lipids, HbA1c, and selected markers of cognitive function and memory,” read the report.

The results on muscle mass were even more profound in the structured exercise group, however. Creatine users who undertook the supervised sessions gained 2.8 pounds of lean mass on average. Creatine was also shown to preserve muscle even under the conditions of fat loss, because participants in the exercise program were given a modest calorie deficit. After 12 weeks, this group had gained almost three pounds of lean tissue despite dropping fat, while the exercise group that took a placebo showed little change in lean tissue. Still, both the structured and non-structured groups, on creatine, saw a greater reduction in body fat percentage than that seen by exercise or diet alone.

“Creatine Monohydrate supplementation with and without exercise and diet intervention may help middle-aged and older adults maintain muscle mass and strength while favorably affecting selected markers of health and cognitive function,” concluded the study.

#8851. How to Master the Run/Walk Method: Using the Magic Mile

You’ve decided to implement the run/walk method into your training and racing strategy. Before you can truly embrace the power of walking during your run routine, you’ll need to take the next step forward: Finding your optimal run/walk paces.

Runners of all levels and backgrounds can find success with the run/walk method, meaning that your run/walk paces and walk interval lengths should be unique to you. With a simple test, you can take guesswork out of your run/walk sessions at the beginning, identify the proper paces for you, and forge a clear path for reaching your training and racing goals.

Runner’s World’s guide, How to Master the Run/Walk Method: Using the Magic Mile, maps out how one helpful test run can define your run/walk training speeds, pace your races strongly, and build fitness for the long term.

In Runner’s World’s How to Master the Run/Walk Method: Using the Magic Mile, we’ll teach you:

Once you have your Magic Mile, use the following formulas created by Galloway to calculate your ideal training and race paces:

An important note to keep in mind: For long runs, your target training pace should be about 90 seconds to two minutes slower than your 5K pace.

Don’t want to do the math? Use our Magic Mile Calculator to find your run/walk training paces with the click of a button.

You should repeat the Magic Mile test every one to three weeks to get the most accurate representation of your fitness and best training paces. When you complete the mile test again, start off slower than your previous pace before gradually speeding up and finishing strong. Over time, you should see the seconds shaving off your time as your fitness progresses.

Once you calculate your run/walk paces with your Magic Mile, begin putting them to use in your training.

Once a week: Complete a tempo run at marathon pace, playing around with different run/walk ratios to find the split that’s most comfortable for you.

Every 1-3 weeks: Repeat the Magic Mile test to adjust your run/walk training paces to your most up-to-date fitness level, especially once you notice you can go farther and feel strong while training at your current paces.

Race day: Ready to conquer your goal race distance? Run your race with the help of the paces you found using the Magic Mile calculator.

Using the training paces determined using your Magic Mile, you can also find your ideal run/walk ratio needed to comfortably hit your unique paces. Run/walk ratio varies by individual, but generally, you can use the following pace guidelines to structure your pacing:

Now, those ratios aren’t inflexible. Once you find the run/walk split outlined for your pace, don’t hesitate to experiment with the lengths of your walking and running segments to find the ratio best for you.

If your Magic Mile is slower than the last time you completed the one-mile run test, don’t panic. Keep track of contributing factors that could be influencing your performance, such as poor sleep and increased stress, among others. A regression could also mean you should focus more on performance-boosting interval sessions, or that you need rest or cross-training.

And while the Magic Mile can serve as a great guideline for informing your training, tracking your fitness, and gauging your optimal race pace, it should be only that.

“[The Magic Mile] gives you an idea of what your goal could be, but I have a lot of runners that I’ve coached who have been able to run faster on race day than what their Magic Mile predicted,” says Chris Twiggs, chief training officer at Galloway Training.

#8850. Common Reasons Diets Stop Working After a While

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Early progress on a weight-loss plan can give way to a stretch where the same effort no longer produces the same results. That shift reflects a set of predictable physiological and behavioral forces that push back against restrictive eating.

Below are nine of those forces and how each one slows progress.

As body weight drops, the body burns fewer calories at rest, partly because it starts conserving energy.

Researchers call this adaptive thermogenesis. A 2026 randomized trial published in the Journal of Human Nutrition and Dietetics detected it within the first week of reduced energy intake. Over time, the same plan produces less progress, even when effort stays consistent.

Weight loss pushes appetite in the wrong direction.

As the body’s energy stores shrink, hunger increases and meals feel less filling. Steeper cuts in food intake intensify both signals, and that pressure makes aggressive restriction hard to sustain.

Banning a food intensifies the desire for it. Eliminating a food works against established habits and social life at the same time, so the plan ends and the banned foods return.

Restrictive weight loss draws energy from muscle as well as fat. Muscle burns energy even at rest, so losing it lowers metabolism further.

A 2025 paper from Reviews in Endocrine & Metabolic Disorders reports that regained weight disproportionately returns as fat rather than as the lean tissue that was lost. The method of weight loss influences how much muscle the body keeps.

In a peer-reviewed randomized controlled trial published in Obesity Science & Practice, participants on the Trilivy™ Reset 5 & 1 Plan retained 98% of lean mass and reduced visceral fat by 14% over 16 weeks.*

“A weight management program that protects lean mass, reduces visceral fat, and builds habit infrastructure is designed for the years after the active weight loss phase and addresses the conditions that drive regain at the source,” said Satya Jonnalagadda, PhD, MBA, RD, Vice President, Scientific & Clinical Affairs at Trilivy.

Constant restriction demands steady mental effort, and a single stressful event can be enough to derail a plan.

Coaching gives people support to continue their plan through stressful periods.

In the same trial from Obesity Science & Practice, participants with coach support lost up to 10 times more weight and 17 times more fat than those in a self-directed group. Trilivy coaches provide accountability and real-time support that help keep a plan on track.

“In a world of automation and AI, human connection is our superpower,” Jonnalagadda said. “A coach can meet a person in the exact moment a routine breaks down, and that is something a notification has never been able to do.”

A pass-fail approach to eating leaves no room for an imperfect meal. Under that framework, deviation from a meal plan feels like a reason to stop, and each restart interrupts the consistency that progress builds on.

Small, untracked additions, like a slightly larger serving or a few bites while cooking, add energy without registering as a meal. Weight loss also prompts the body to reduce spontaneous movement, which lowers daily energy use.

Both shifts happen gradually, and together they slow progress.

In a 2026 study from Annals of Internal Medicine, adults who slept about 80 minutes less per night gained roughly a pound and became more sedentary over six weeks. Their weight gain tracked closely with the drop in daily movement.

The finding connects short sleep to reduced activity, one of the everyday inputs a weight-loss plan relies on.

Restaurant meals, birthdays, work events, and holidays bring menus, timing and traditions that differ from an established meal plan.

Rules designed around a home kitchen do not offer guidance for those moments. A plan that accounts for eating out and celebrations gives people a way to navigate them.

Each of these nine factors traces back to two pressures: a body that works to protect its energy stores and daily routines that strict rules don’t account for.

A sustainable approach to weight management addresses both. It protects lean muscle, pairs balanced nutrition and physical activity with healthy daily habits, and builds in coaching and accountability that continue past the initial results, supporting long-term metabolic health.

Trilivy™ recommends that you contact your healthcare provider before starting and throughout your weight loss journey.

* Arterburn LM, et al. Randomized controlled trial assessing two commercial weight loss programs in adults with overweight or obesity. Obesity Science & Practice. 2019. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/osp4.312. In a clinical study, individuals on the Reset 5 & 1 Plan experienced a reduction of 14% visceral fat and 98% of lean mass was retained at 16 weeks. Those on the Reset 5 & 1 Plan with the support of a coach lost up to 10x more weight and 17x more fat than those who tried to lose weight on their own.

#8849. The 2026 New York City Marathon Was the Largest Marathon in History

More than 61,000 runners—from ages 18 to 90—crossed the finish line on Sunday.

One of the world's biggest marathons keeps getting bigger. On Sunday, November 1, the 2026 New York City Marathon officially cemented its place in the history books as the largest marathon of all time, surpassing the 2026 London Marathon, which had 59,830 finishers.

According to results released Monday by New York Road Runners (NYRR), 61,146 runners crossed the iconic finish line in Central Park (61,529 started the event). That total blasts past last year’s NYC tally of 59,226 finishers—which followed 2024’s record-breaking field of 55,646—marking the third consecutive year the five-borough race has raised the bar worldwide for mass participation.

This year’s record served as a nice topper for a historic run as it coincided with the 50th anniversary of the five-borough course. When organizers first took the race out of Central Park and onto the streets of Staten Island, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx, and Manhattan in 1976, the event was a bold urban experiment. Five decades later, it is an epicenter of the global running community, with waves of marathoners streaming from the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge from 8 a.m. until well after dark.

While tens of thousands of age-groupers, charity runners, and first-timers chased personal glory, the pro fields delivered plenty of fireworks at the front of the pack:

There were plenty of other milestones as well.

#8847. A 24-Year-Old Runner Died After a Medical Emergency in the Final Miles of the NYC Marathon

Rachel Apa was running her first marathon to raise money for Parkinson's research in memory of her grandfather.

Rachel Apa was nearing the end of her first New York City Marathon when she collapsed in Central Park on Sunday, November 1. The 24-year-old had spent months putting in the work needed to conquer 26.2 miles, but never made it across the finish line. Instead, she was taken to Mount Sinai Medical Center, where she died later that night.

Apa, a Bucknell University alum who lived in central Pennsylvania, came to New York to run with Parkinson's Foundation Champions, raising money in memory of her grandfather, who died from the disease in 2022.

According to reporting from The New York Times, the medical emergency happened around 1:30 p.m. close to Mile 24, around 85th Street, right as runners enter the final stretch through Central Park. Several spectators rushed to help and began performing CPR. New York Road Runners medical staff arrived shortly after, and tried to resuscitate her with a defibrillator before paramedics took her to the hospital.

Her parents had been keeping up with Rachel throughout the race as she made her way through the five boroughs, though from different locations. Michelle Apa, her mother, was in New York and watched Rachel run through Queens at Mile 14, while Steve Apa, her father, was back home in Lewisberry, Pennsylvania, following her progress through the marathon's tracking app.

Steve had been texting his daughter throughout the day. According to messages he shared with the Times, Rachel sent an "Ow" text at Mile 18, followed by a double "Ow ow" at Mile 19. She kept moving through the course, although her dad received no replies after that. As she reached Mile 23 on the app, Steve sent another message: "Final stretch." Rachel never responded.

Michelle eventually made her way to Central Park, reportedly arriving just as the ambulance carrying her daughter was leaving, per the Times. Doctors spent hours trying to save Rachel. Steve told the newspaper she was pronounced dead around 9:40 p.m.

"It's unfathomable," he told the newspaper. "Perfect health, perfect shape, 24 years old."

Steve told the Times that his daughter died from rhabdomyolysis, which occurs when damaged muscle tissue breaks down and releases substances into the bloodstream. The condition can cause serious kidney damage and, according to the Cleveland Clinic, can be triggered by extreme physical exertion.

An official cause of death had not been established as of Tuesday, November 3, with CBS New York reporting that the city's medical examiner was still investigating.

Sunday marked the marathon's first runner death following a medical incident since 2024, according to NYRR. The organization released a statement Monday:

"We are deeply saddened by the death of one of our runners following yesterday's race. Our thoughts and sincere sympathies are with the runner's family, friends, and the entire running community."

Before the marathon, Apa explained her decision to run on her fundraising page, sharing how much her grandfather influenced her love of sports and why supporting the Parkinson's Foundation mattered to her.

"He taught me to stay active, push my limits, and embrace challenges, shaping my love for sports and movement," she wrote.

Apa explained that watching him lose his mobility after his Parkinson's diagnosis had made her want to help others facing the disease. She wanted to use her first marathon to help others affected by it, raising money and awareness in the process “for research, better care, and a cure.”

As of 5 p.m. ET Tuesday, the page had exceeded her $4,000 goal, and reflected more than $28,000 in donations.

Sean Abrams was the Senior Editor, Growth and Engagement at Men’s Health. He’s a former hip hop dancer who likes long walks on the beach and large glasses of tequila. You can find his previous work at Maxim, Elite Daily, and AskMen.

#8845. The 7 Best Jogging Strollers for Every Active Parent

These strollers combine comfort, convenience, and style. They’re perfect for moms and dads trying to get a workout in.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Getting out for a run as a parent of a little one is made infinitely easier with a great jogging stroller. As a running mom, I spent countless hours behind my kids, and now my nieces and nephews lacing up and getting behind a stroller for my own mental and physical health and giving my siblings a much-needed respite (I even bring back treats).

I’ve since made running my job, and have had the opportunity to test dozens of running strollers over the years, and let me tell you, they are not all the same. The range of quality and ride between them can be pretty bananas, and as someone who tends toward higher mileage, it took me a long time to find one that I loved.

Thankfully, jogging strollers have evolved a lot since my first runs with my baby over a decade ago, and now there is a great jogging stroller for everyone no matter your height, running style, surfaces you run on, or miles you’ll be logging. There are strollers that work as both running and everyday strollers, luxury running strollers, multisport strollers that can hit the snow, be towed by a bicycle, or pushed on your own steam, and there are high-tech jogging strollers ready to rack up at the races.

Every year, I dedicate hundreds of hours to testing jogging strollers. I run with kids aged roughly 7 months to 3 years on tracks, pavement, highly groomed trails, boardwalks, and even those charming New York sidewalks. Each stroller clocks at least 40 miles under my watch through all sorts of conditions—rain, snow, sunshine, you name it, we’re out there. Snack testing is a must for cleanability checks, naturally.

Storage? I’ve crammed everything imaginable into the baskets on these. Brakes get a relentless workout. I've folded, unfolded, and hauled these things all over the tri-state area. Airports? Been there, done that (huge mistake, by the way). Here’s my travel tip: check it in a stroller travel bag and thank me later.

Beyond the specs, it’s about the feel. How easy is it to push and steer, even one-handed? And since my nieces and nephews are my precious cargo, their comfort is paramount. We log countless miles, and I see firsthand how happy they are (or aren’t) in each stroller. Some provide a dream ride, others unleash their inner tiny terrors. Basically, I get the real 411 on what works and what doesn't.

Thule makes some of the best tech and outdoor gear on the market, and this stroller is a shining example of the brand. It’s somehow both rugged and elegant, providing the runner with easy, light-touch steering and braking. I was a huge fan of the two previous iterations of this stroller, but this version has surpassed my expectations. I always had issues with the length and size of the canopy, and the tilted position of the seat. But this version sits more upright and has a more generous canopy than its predecessors, making it more comfortable for your little one.

The pneumatic tires are fab and give the stroller a lot of give to glide over difficult terrain like boardwalks, bumpy tracks, and even some trails. I took this beast out on the jankiest boardwalk in all of the land—Rockaway Beach in Queens, New York, and not only did my little nephew fall asleep and stay asleep (and secure) in the stroller even as I almost tripped a dozen times, he fell asleep so deeply that he actually transferred from the stroller to the car seat without a stir.

The storage basket is a decent size, but I do wish it was mesh material, which sand and other dirt could fall through. Also, given that it’s a solid fabric and not mesh, I’d expect it to have a larger weight limit. As it is, 15 pounds is all you can carry beneath. That being said, there are tons of accessories, including handle bags that increase storage capacity and convenience.

I love the twisting hand brake on the Thule. It is a less-abrupt stop than a traditional hand brake, giving you more control. The foot brake is easily operated as well, though disengaging the brakes should not be done in sandals or bare feet.

As for the car seat attachment and available bassinet, both are great, but they do come at an extra price, and the Thule UG3 is bulky for every day. However, it’s such a nice ride, and since the front wheel locks in place and unlocks for easy turning, it is usable as an everyday stroller.

Finding any stroller for under $200 is a feat, especially right now. For families on a budget, the Baby Trend Expedition Jogger is a fantastic option that doesn’t skimp on features. Surprisingly, it includes multiple parent and child drink trays, an accessory often sold separately with more expensive models, adding a bit of convenience. (However, when running, skip the hard cups for the toddlers for safety.)

For the price, the ride is smooth and capable of handling casual jogs and everyday outings. However, it’s worth noting that the overall build quality and components feel a bit flimsier compared to higher-end strollers. The fabrics are a bit scratchier, and the frame and accessories are just not the same.

That said, it’s still a solid stroller with a lot of potential for families. It’s probably not going to withstand the same high mileage or rigorous use as its pricier counterparts, but it’s ideal for those with less intense running routines. Also, it’s specifically designed to be compatible with Baby Trend infant car seats, which is something to keep in mind when considering your overall travel system.

So you don’t want to store a stroller for every occasion? I get it. I live in Brooklyn and understand the limits of small spaces. Enter the solution to your problems: The Guava Roam is a fabulous compact everyday and jogging stroller known for its easy maneuverability and relatively compact fold. It features broad car seat compatibility via its adapters for various brands including Graco, Nuna, UppaBaby, Cybex, Chicco, and Britax. It has one of the smallest footprints both folded and unfolded, and while it’s a bit on the heavy side at 28.5 pounds, the way it folds makes it easy to lug around and stash in your trunk.

But the diminutive size and convenience aren’t the only things that make this an outstanding option for families and runners. My favorite bit about this stroller is the fact that you can lock and unlock the front wheel via a control at the handlebar. It’s genius. I have no earthly clue why more stroller companies aren’t doing this.

I’m also a huge fan of the independent suspension on this stroller that settles and levels as you hit large divots, giving the passenger a smooth, easy ride.

The seat on this stroller is our 3-year-old tester’s favorite, with the five-point harness that’s “not pinchy” and the seat “nice on your booty.” I like the accessory kit near the adjustable handlebar that fits your drink, your phone, your wallet, and at least four mini bags of gummy Nerd clusters (my running fuel of choice).

The stroller isn’t perfect, but it’s so good, you can almost overlook the shallow undercarriage basket and the fact it’s lacking a hand brake. Ideally, I’d love for this stroller to also have pneumatic tires for longer runs and better shock absorption, but the whole thing is just so convenient, its positives easily outweigh its negatives.

I’ve hauled about a gajillion strollers in and out of car trunks, and I know which ones claim to be compact when folded, and which really are. The Cybex Avi Spin is actually a compact jogging stroller. It has a unique way of folding that allows you to either do a basic, one-handed compact fold, or go all the way, and remove the tires first, and then fold it into something that’s around backpack-sized.

The ride is lovely for the jogger, with an adjustable handlebar (it requires two hands to adjust), soft, moisture-wicking grip, and lockable front wheel with an easy deceleration hand brake. It coasts over ruts and bumps really well, but it’s by no means going to hit any trails and remain stable. Jogging strollers aren’t really built for that, by and large.

It cleans up beautifully as well, with removable, machine-washable fabrics, including the UPF 50+-rated canopy. Just pretreat the fabric, wash on gentle, and lay flat to dry.

I do have one gripe, though, and it’s not nothing. The ergonomic, nearly lie-flat seat is fantastic for naps, and the no-rethread, easy-to-adjust harness is great, but younger passengers will lose most of the view if they’re reclined even a little purely because of positioning. This is common on many strollers, but for some reason, is more pronounced on this model. Our tester cared not at all, though, as he was busy looking straight out at the flock of American oystercatchers gathered on the boardwalk at the beach in Queens, New York, where I tested this stroller. My suggestion? Find a running area with dopey looking birds and kids are thrilled. Egrets are also a favorite, I’ve found.

I am a massive fan of this double stroller—Bob gets it right with this one. It’s largely one of the easiest to assemble and to fold, whether or not you take off the wheels. It’s a joy to push, even if you have two large toddlers in the seats. The tires are my favorite of any standard jogging stroller on this list. They are the best aligned, and the adjustable front wheel means you never have to worry if it comes out of alignment, as you can just fix it in a few tweaks.

But oh, how I could write sonnets about the storage. You know what you need a ton of when you’re pushing two kids for a two-plus hour run? Everything. Diapers, wipes, snacks, drinks, extra clothing, sunscreen, snacks for yourself, a few bottles of water, and more. And with the giant storage basket and all the storage cubbies on this beauty, you’ve got the space to hold them. The only thing it doesn’t store is extra patience for when they start fighting at mile 10 and you have 3.1 more miles on your run.

I have run over 200 miles with this stroller, and though I have had to replace the inner tube in the front tire, the stroller is still in great shape. The combination mesh and sealed poly storage basket underneath has seen some things in its life, and it still comes out clean and doesn’t smell, which is a huge accomplishment considering all it has been through.

While lugging it around folded isn't the easiest task, the Bob Revolution 3.0 Duallie’s exceptional performance and ample storage more than compensate. Overall, this double stroller is a top pick for parents who love to run and need the capacity for two little ones. It’s a durable, comfortable, and thoughtfully designed stroller that will make countless runs a joy for both you and your children.

I had heaps of fun testing this stroller out, and recently, I even got on a bicycle (not my thing!) and tried it out in tow mode. This stroller is a beast and, truly, it is only for the most sporting amongst us. If you’re a serious outdoor fanatic, you’ve met your match. It’s designed like a bike trailer, but thanks to its multiple bases/setups, it works as a stroller, a jogging stroller, a bike trailer, and even a stroller on skis for snowshoeing and fun in the sand.

This is technically the double version, but I think it’s worth it to get the wider Chariot Cross 2 over the single version, as it feels a bit more stable than the single, and gives your child some extra space. The seats inside are roomy, and I had no complaints from the Peanut Section about the straps or cushion levels, no matter if the kids were being towed, pushed, or shoved over ice and snow.

Switching the kits out could be simpler, but it’s not especially difficult. I managed to do it pretty easily, and I have a partially paralyzed left hand. Putting it together initially is honestly a bigger pain. It’s easy to clean, though, with removable pads. The materials can take a serious amount of scrubbing and hosing off without showing any wear, which is good considering how filthy a stroller like this could become.

I love the oversized storage bag that affixes to the back. It’s simple to use and clean, and deep enough to fit way more than you’d expect. It’s a slick feature that puts this stroller in a category of its own.

As for the ride, it’s as smooth as it can be over the snow, sand, and ice. This stroller is a bit heavy for an all-out run, but great for jogging slow, easy miles. As a regular stroller, it’s great for myriad applications, but my favorite way to use it is when you’re in a buggy area, as it’s completely enclosed. As a bike trailer, it shines, holding its ground and keeping everything steady. For serious outdoor enthusiasts seeking a versatile and durable multisport option, the Thule Chariot Cross 2 is a top-tier choice that's built to handle almost any adventure.

I’ve pushed the Veer Switch&Jog over 25 miles on all kinds of terrain, and it did well on almost everything. I struggled to push it on mud and sand, but that’s true of just about any stroller. The second I find one that doesn’t? You’ll be the first to know.

My favorite thing about this baby is that you’re able to switch out the jump seat back and forth. Additional pieces are available. The cooler is great, and the booster seat takes about two seconds to set up at a restaurant, which freaking rocks when you think about how dirty restaurant high chairs can get.

During the testing we had a projectile vomit situation. Totally my fault. I overfed the small human treats before the run. My bad, I know better. I took it straight to a self-serve car wash and sprayed absolute crap out of it with the a high-pressure wand. After a little scrubbing, it was totally fine, and the smell came out too (thank god, because it was dairy). I do wish the fabric was machine washable, but it’s attached so firmly to the frame that I get why it’s not.

On runs, it’s stable, and the telescoping handle and handbrake are both easy to use. The front wheel locks for straightaways and unlocks when you’re just wandering around the city.

Folding it is kind of a pain in the you-know-what, not gonna lie. But it’s a convertible tank of a stroller, and it’s very hard to beat at this price.

Given that jogging strollers can be a significant investment, it's crucial to select one that aligns with your needs. To ensure you choose the right stroller, consider these key specifications:

These specs directly relate to your running style. Serious runners will prioritize performance features like wheel type and suspension, while casual joggers might focus on convenience features like car seat compatibility and ease of folding.

To be included on this list, every jogging stroller must meet certain criteria. Key features of a good jogging stroller include a lockable front wheel for safe straightaways at a running pace, excellent build quality for durability, a large canopy for sun protection, and built-in safety features such as a wrist strap, sweat-resistant handlebar grips, and a secure harness system.

And, not for nothing, but they need to feel good when you run behind them. I can’t tell you how many clunkers I’ve tested that made my runs a chore. They need to provide both the runner and the passenger with a comfortable experience. If you’re kicking the storage basket or your hands feel like they’ve become permanently glued to the handlebar, you’re not going to want to use that stroller.

As avid runners who have embraced parenthood, we understand the unique demands placed on jogging strollers. We know that these aren't just tools for transporting children; they are crucial pieces of equipment that must perform flawlessly whether you're engaged in rigorous training for your next marathon or simply navigating the everyday errands with your little one in tow.

For years, the Runner's World team has been committed to guiding runners toward the gear that allows them to achieve peak performance and enjoy their passion for running to the max. This deep-seated expertise extends into our in-depth evaluations of running gear, and jogging strollers are no exception. Our primary objective is to thoroughly test and identify the options available on the market, and to provide informed and reliable recommendations for runners of all experience levels.

When is it safe to run with your child in the stroller?

The general rule recommended by pediatricians is to wait until the baby is at least 6 months old, and has good head, trunk, and neck control. AKA, they can sit unassisted for long periods of time.

What is the best way to clean a jogging stroller?

Honestly, some of these strollers allow you to remove many of the fabrics and wash them in the machine, but for a jogger, it’s kind of a pain. I suggest taking off the canopy, tilting the whole thing upside down and shaking it out before using a damp cloth and wiping it down, and allowing it to air dry. If it’s really gross, hose the thing down, but take off the harness first, as soaking it can reduce its efficacy.

What Should You Avoid in a jogging stroller?

You should be holding your child’s hard sippy cups and snacks and save those for walking breaks. Jogging can jostle, and I’ve seen some pretty gnarly dental injuries on kids who had plastic sippy cup incidents from jogging strollers.

Generally not. Even if they fall within the parameters set by Disney of 31- by 52 inches, I’ve heard of many of them (apart from the Guava) getting rejected at the gates.

Cat Bowen, senior editor of commerce; reviews, is a seasoned runner with more than 20 years of distance running experience, including dozens of marathons, half marathons, and even a few ultra marathons. For over a decade, she has tested parenting, fitness, home, and running gear and written in-depth guides to help readers with their next purchase.
